learning_science.concrete_decision: Pair dot groups and length bars with varied equation forms, then fade some concrete support while retaining the relational balance cue.
learning_science.source: Rittle-Johnson, B., & Alibali, M. W. (1999). Conceptual and procedural knowledge of mathematics: Does one lead to the other? Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(1), 175-189.

learning_science.principle: Arithmetic and early algebra can be integrated through relational thinking about equality and operation properties
learning_science.why: Commuting, decomposing, and compensating quantities reveal algebra-ready structure without letter symbols.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Escalate from direct matching to compensation, decomposition, repeated groups, and equivalence transformations while keeping values visually grounded.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, T. P., Franke, M. L., & Levi, L. (2003). Thinking Mathematically: Integrating Arithmetic and Algebra in Elementary School. Heinemann.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EQREL uses the first substantive choice to distinguish a relational solution from operational total-all or answer-after-equals signatures. M-ERRTYPE preserves compensation, inverse-operation, side-confusion, and near-miss evidence, while M-REV records spontaneous correction before commit without requiring an explanation. M-DIFFREACH marks the most structurally non-canonical equivalence handled and M-LEARNRATE captures transfer as concrete bars fade, sharpening tail placement beyond arithmetic accuracy alone.
age_rationale: The type begins at grades 2-3 because the equal and join/remove symbols are the minimal notation being assessed; dot groups, bars, and the balance backdrop prevent reading or numeral fluency from being prerequisites. Grades 4-5 add varied unknown positions and operations on both sides; grades 6-8 add compensation, repeated groups, and nested visual operations without letters. All responses use large tiles, never typed numerals.

adaptive.content_range: small dot-group non-canonical equalities through multi-operation compensation, decomposition, repeated-group, and unknown-position equivalence structures
difficulty_levers: one versus multiple operations across both sides
concrete quantity support and degree of fading
compensation, decomposition, inverse, or repeated-group structure
adaptive.notes: Generate two equal expression trees, mask one leaf or group, and produce distractors from documented operational strategies. Strategy-aware adaptation samples parallel forms to confirm M-EQREL before escalating structural depth, keeping arithmetic values small relative to the equivalence demand.

engagement_hook: Every solved equality steadies a glowing bridge between two islands, making same-on-both-sides physically satisfying.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Prior worksheet format can bias children toward operational responding; varied layouts and the wordless relational demo mitigate familiarity without coaching scored answers. Arithmetic fact difficulty must remain below structural difficulty, and bars must not directly reveal an answer option through pixel matching. Use texture plus color, large snap slots, no time bonus, and log accidental swaps separately from conceptual revisions. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Biggest Number
topics_techniques_covered: number_properties_reasoning: arrange quantity or digit tiles to create the largest or smallest possible value
number_properties_reasoning: satisfy visual even-odd, equal-group factor, divisibility, and multi-constraint conditions while optimizing value
number_sense_magnitude: compose and compare place-value quantities using ones, groups, and positional magnitude
quantitative_comparison: reason about which placement or swap increases, decreases, or preserves the constructed value
one_liner: The child rearranges quantity tiles to build the biggest or smallest value that obeys the pictured rules.
interaction: A row of large cards and ordered place slots appears beside a goal icon: a tall mountain for largest or a small burrow for smallest. The child drags cards into slots or taps a card then a slot, can swap freely, and taps GO. K-1 cards are dot towers placed into two magnitude lanes; later bands use digit cards paired with place-value blocks, while pair icons and equal-group trays convey even-odd or factor constraints without words or typed input.
self_teach: In a wordless demo under 10 seconds, the ghost hand swaps a larger dot tower into the left high-value lane; the built magnitude bar grows and the mountain glows. One unscored two-card warm-up follows, and if reversed, the bars compare and the hand demonstrates the better swap before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Number sense develops through an integrated structure linking quantity, counting, comparison, and place value
learning_science.why: Optimization is meaningful only when the child understands that a card's position changes its contribution to the whole.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Begin with visible quantity lanes, pair later digit positions with base-unit blocks, and fade those supports as place-value reasoning stabilizes.
learning_science.source: Case, R., & Griffin, S. (1990). Child cognitive development: The role of central conceptual structures in the development of scientific and social thought. In C.-A. Hauert (Ed.), Developmental Psychology: Cognitive, Perceptuo-Motor, and Neurological Perspectives, 193-230. North-Holland.

learning_science.principle: Learning trajectories organize increasingly sophisticated mathematical actions around a stable goal
learning_science.why: The same arrange-and-compare shell can progress from direct magnitude to positional value and interacting number constraints.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Route from two concrete quantities to multi-place optimization, then add one and later several visually demonstrated property constraints.
learning_science.source: Clements, D. H., & Sarama, J. (2004). Learning trajectories in mathematics education. Mathematical Thinking and Learning, 6(2), 81-89.

learning_science.principle: Overlapping-waves theory highlights diverse strategies and increasingly adaptive choice among them
learning_science.why: Children may exhaustively try arrangements, place the largest card first, reason from the units constraint backward, or coordinate all constraints.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log the full swap path and score systematic constraint-first or place-value-first planning against redundant trial-and-error.
learning_science.source: Siegler, R. S. (1996). Emerging Minds: The Process of Change in Children's Thinking. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PATH and M-PLANFUL reveal whether the child prioritizes the most valuable slot, satisfies a restrictive units condition first, and avoids redundant permutations. M-EFF compares the swap sequence with an optimal construction path, while M-ERRTYPE distinguishes reversed place value, local-greedy, parity, factor, and missed-constraint solutions. M-DIFFREACH records maximum slots and simultaneous properties coordinated, and M-LEARNRATE captures rapid strategy improvement as new pictorial constraints are introduced.
age_rationale: K-1 uses two countable dot towers and two visually unequal place lanes, so no digit reading, property vocabulary, or precise dragging is needed. Grades 2-3 add two- and three-place digit cards with base-unit overlays and a pictured pair/no-leftover condition; grades 4-5 add several cards and one factor or parity constraint; grades 6-8 coordinate largest-smallest goals with multiple divisibility or equal-group constraints. Tap-then-slot is always available as a motor alternative.

adaptive.content_range: ordering two concrete quantities at K-1 through optimizing multi-place values under interacting parity, equal-group factor, divisibility, repetition, or fixed-position constraints
difficulty_levers: number of cards and place slots
largest versus smallest or bounded-target goal
quantity cards versus digits with fading place-value support
number of feasible arrangements and proximity of the runner-up
adaptive.notes: Enumerate all card permutations under generated constraints to guarantee a unique optimum or explicitly score ties. Create misconception-keyed near-optimal foils and adapt by slot count, support fading, and constraint count rather than by obscure number facts.

engagement_hook: The constructed value becomes a tower: smart swaps make it shoot upward toward the mountain or shrink neatly into the burrow while rule badges click into place.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Digit recognition and learned divisibility rules can become a knowledge barrier, so early items use quantity overlays and every property icon is self-taught through concrete pairs or equal groups. Do not use reading, color-only constraints, or tiny drag slots. Ensure animation does not expose the optimum before submission, keep search spaces age-appropriate, and treat repeated exploratory swaps as process evidence rather than a motor penalty. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Story Model
topics_techniques_covered: word_problem_reasoning: build a manipulable situation model for join, separate, compare, equal-group, sharing, and multi-step quantity stories
arithmetic_reasoning: derive an unknown quantity from pictured actions and relations without relying on written operation notation
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: coordinate quantities, unknown position, grouping, comparison, and multiple constraints in a visual story
one_liner: The child rebuilds a silent quantity story with objects or bars and uses the model to find what is missing.
interaction: A brief replayable animation shows objects joining, leaving, being compared, grouped, or shared; the final state contains a glowing question space. The child drags or tap-places objects and resizable unit bars into a model area, then taps the resulting quantity tile and GO. All story details are conveyed by motion and icons, every quantity remains visible on replay, and no prose, operation string, explanation, or typed numeral is required.
self_teach: In a wordless demo under 10 seconds, two birds land beside three birds; the ghost hand places matching two- and three-unit bars end to end, taps the five-object result, and both story and model glow. One unscored join warm-up follows with an unlimited replay and a corrective model-build animation after an error.

learning_science.principle: Solving arithmetic stories depends on constructing a situation model of the quantitative relations
learning_science.why: Keyword matching is insufficient when the unknown changes position or several relations interact.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the child's intermediate object or bar model, vary semantic schemas and unknown positions, and keep the animation replayable so comprehension can be separated from memory.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W., & Greeno, J. G. (1985). Understanding and solving word arithmetic problems. Psychological Review, 92(1), 109-129.

learning_science.principle: Grounded representations can support quantitative reasoning when formal equations are harder to comprehend
learning_science.why: Objects, actions, and bars let children express relation structure without translating into algebraic notation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require model construction before answer selection and escalate relational depth while avoiding written equations or operation vocabulary.
learning_science.source: Koedinger, K. R., & Nathan, M. J. (2004). The real story behind story problems: Effects of representations on quantitative reasoning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(2), 129-164.

learning_science.principle: Cognitively guided instruction research shows that children's strategies vary systematically with problem structure
learning_science.why: Join, separate, part-whole, compare, equal-group, and sharing situations elicit different valid models and reveal reasoning beyond a final answer.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Generate across semantic problem classes and score model structure and path, allowing multiple mathematically valid strategies rather than enforcing one operation sequence.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, T. P., Fennema, E., Franke, M. L., Levi, L., & Empson, S. B. (1999). Children's Mathematics: Cognitively Guided Instruction. Heinemann.

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY grades whether the model captures the entities, grouping, direction of change, comparison relation, and final answer even when one component is wrong. M-PATH, M-PROG, and M-PLANFUL distinguish direct situation modeling, systematic bar construction, and useful decomposition from answer guessing or unstructured manipulation. M-DIFFREACH records the deepest semantic and multistep structure solved, while M-LEARNRATE tracks transfer across unfamiliar visual stories, yielding tail information that a written word-problem score would lose to reading variance.
age_rationale: The type begins at grades 2-3 because preserving a story relation while constructing a separate model requires more coordination than the K-1 catalog should assume, even with no reading. Grades 2-3 use one-step join, separate, compare, or equal-group animations with small quantities; grades 4-5 vary unknown position and add two steps; grades 6-8 coordinate nested groups, rates, remainders, and multiple constraints through bars and objects. Replay, large pieces, and tap placement reduce memory and motor demands.

adaptive.content_range: one-step concrete join, separate, compare, grouping, and sharing situations through multi-step, unknown-first, nested-group, rate, remainder, and multi-constraint visual models
difficulty_levers: number of sequential or nested relations
object model versus more compressed bar model
number of valid intermediate strategies and constraint interactions
adaptive.notes: Generate a latent situation graph first, render it as animation and manipulatives, and solve the graph to validate all accepted models and answers. Strategy-aware adaptation samples new semantic shells rather than merely larger numbers, with partial states automatically scored and replay available throughout.

engagement_hook: Tiny animated stories pause at a mystery moment, and the child becomes the scene builder whose model makes the ending play out.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Animation comprehension, cultural familiarity, and working memory can contaminate quantitative reasoning; use universal objects and actions, no speech or text, unlimited replay, and stable camera framing. Avoid irrelevant decorative characters, color-only grouping, tiny pieces, and story timing pressure. Multiple valid models must receive equal credit, and quantities should stay easy enough that relational modeling - not fact recall - sets difficulty. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Explorer's Map
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking: after exploring, the child points from their current position and heading toward a landmark they can no longer see, requiring an allocentric survey representation
mazes_route_planning: the child finds an efficient route through a partly hidden world and, at the end, chooses or traces a shortcut they never actually travelled
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child explores a foggy top-down world that reveals only what is nearby, then shows they built a map in their head by pointing back toward hidden landmarks and taking a shortcut they never walked.
interaction: A top-down world is covered in fog that clears only around the child's avatar as they tap adjacent tiles to walk, uncovering paths and landmarks (a tree, a well, home). After collecting the landmarks the fog returns and a compass dial appears: the child drags the dial to point toward an icon-named landmark from where they now stand (repeated for a few landmarks), then taps the route they think is the shortest way home. Taps to move and a drag dial to point; no typing, no reading. Path, exploration and pointing angles are logged.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand walks the avatar two tiles to uncover a tree, then swings the compass dial to point back at the tree with an arrow, so 'explore, then point where it is' is obvious in under 10s. One unscored warm-up on a tiny 3x3 world with one landmark runs, showing the correct arrow gently if missed, before scored worlds begin.

learning_science.principle: Cognitive maps and survey knowledge
learning_science.why: Beyond following a known route, forming an allocentric survey map of an environment is a distinct, higher spatial ability that predicts real-world navigation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The world is revealed only locally so success requires integrating pieces into a survey map, then pointing to unseen landmarks tests that map directly.
learning_science.source: Tolman, E. C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review, 55(4), 189-208.

learning_science.principle: Route-to-survey developmental progression
learning_science.why: Children progress from landmark and route knowledge to configural survey knowledge; measuring novel-shortcut choice and pointing error isolates where a child sits on that progression.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A never-travelled shortcut and hidden-landmark pointing are used because they can only be solved with survey (not route) knowledge.
learning_science.source: Siegel, A. W., & White, S. H. (1975). The development of spatial representations of large-scale environments. Advances in Child Development and Behavior, 10, 9-55.

tail_precision_rationale: M-VIEWANG (angular error when pointing to hidden landmarks) is a continuous, ceiling-resistant survey-knowledge signal that separates strong cognitive mappers from route-followers far better than a solved/unsolved bit, and its systematic component exposes residual egocentric bias. M-EFF (shortcut length versus the true shortest never-travelled path) and M-EXPLORE (how efficiently the world was uncovered) add planful-exploration signal, and M-DIFFREACH marks the largest world mapped at criterion.
age_rationale: Allocentric survey mapping and pointing to unseen places emerge around age 5+, so the richest signal is at 4-5 and 6-8; 2-3 is included with tiny worlds and mostly egocentric, in-view pointing, while K-1 is excluded because reliable allocentric pointing is not yet developed. Larger worlds, more landmarks and forced shortcuts raise demand for older bands. Tap-to-move avoids fine motor and there is no reading.

adaptive.content_range: tiny worlds with one in-view landmark (2-3) up to large multi-landmark worlds requiring hidden-landmark pointing and novel shortcuts (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: amount of the world that stays hidden
number and offset of pointing targets
whether the shortcut was ever traversed
adaptive.notes: Worlds are procedurally generated with known landmark coordinates so pointing error and shortest-path optimality are computed automatically; unlimited parallel maps and above-level world sizes for ceiling probing.

engagement_hook: Uncovering a foggy world tile by tile and finding secret shortcuts is an explorer's-treasure hook, and a star rating for accurate pointing and short routes drives replay.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large tiles and a drag dial keep motor demands low; fog clears generously so the task measures map-building not visual acuity; landmarks are distinct icons not colour-only; the ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; score pointing accuracy and route efficiency, not speed, so deliberate explorers are not penalised; keep worlds small enough that working-memory load reflects mapping ability rather than raw storage limits at young bands. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Star Filter
topics_techniques_covered: selective_filtering: the child holds in mind only the target-coloured shapes while ignoring distractors, then reports them after a delay (filter-and-remember)
updating_binding: as new items stream in, the child updates which items belong to which slot/feature, binding item to location
attention_control: sustaining attention on relevant items and suppressing salient distractors over the trial
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child watches a brief array, remembers only the target-coloured shapes (ignoring the rest), and after a short blank taps where those shapes were.
interaction: A cue shows the target colour, then several shapes (targets plus distractors) flash briefly and disappear. After a short blank the child taps the grid cells where the target-coloured shapes had been (tap again to deselect), then taps DONE. The number of targets and distractors scales the load. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches two blue and one grey shape flash, then after the blank taps only the two cells where blue had been, which light green - under 10s, showing you keep only the target colour. One unscored warm-up with one target and one distractor runs before scored higher-load trials begin.

learning_science.principle: Attentional control of access to working memory
learning_science.why: High-capacity individuals differ mainly in excluding irrelevant items from working memory, not in raw storage.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors must be filtered out before the delayed report, so the score reflects filtering efficiency, the individual-difference driver.
learning_science.source: Vogel, E. K., McCollough, A. W., & Machizawa, M. G. (2005). Neural measures reveal individual differences in controlling access to working memory. Nature 438.

learning_science.principle: Executive attention view of working-memory capacity
learning_science.why: Working-memory capacity is largely the ability to control attention and resist interference.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Salient distractors and a retention delay load executive attention, so the task indexes controlled attention rather than passive span.
learning_science.source: Engle, R. W. (2002). Working memory capacity as executive attention. Current Directions in Psychological Science 11(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-DPRIME separates true filtering sensitivity from guessing (a cautious child and a guesser are not scored alike), and M-FALSEALARM specifically counts distractor intrusions, the purest filtering-failure signal. M-UPDATECOST (accuracy decrement per added distractor) and M-SPAN (staircased target load at criterion) give a continuous capacity estimate that keeps separating high performers who all succeed at low load.
age_rationale: Watch-then-tap-where-it-was is accessible from 2-3 with one target and one distractor and generous timing. 4-5 raises target and distractor counts; 6-8 uses high distractor loads and shorter exposures that separate efficient filterers. Large tap cells and a colour-plus-shape target cue avoid motor and colour-vision confounds; no reading.

adaptive.content_range: one-target one-distractor arrays with long exposure (2-3) up to high-distractor-load brief arrays (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Arrays are procedurally sampled with target load staircased for M-SPAN and distractor count varied for M-UPDATECOST; parallel forms are unlimited and consistency clones support near-cut checks.

engagement_hook: A quick catch-the-stars memory flash with lights and a satisfying reveal keeps children leaning in, and rising loads feel like harder arcade waves.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Targets are cued by colour plus a shape/pattern for colour-vision fairness; large tap cells remove motor demands; timing is tuned per band so processing speed does not contaminate the capacity estimate; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; M-DPRIME corrects for guessing so response bias does not inflate scores. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Path Forge
topics_techniques_covered: manipulation: the child rotates and places road tiles, mentally and physically transforming pieces to line up a connected route
spatial_navigation: the assembled road defines a route from the start hut to the goal that a courier then walks
planning_lookahead: connecting the road without wasted tiles requires ordering placements several steps ahead
problem_solving: build one continuous coin-collecting path under a tile budget, a spatial constraint-satisfaction goal
mazes_route_planning: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
mental_rotation: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child rotates and drops road tiles to build one continuous path from the start hut to the goal, then the courier walks the route.
interaction: A grid shows a start hut, a goal flag and some blocked cells, with a tray of road tiles (straight, curve, T). The child taps a tile then taps an empty cell to place it, taps a placed tile to rotate it or remove it, building a connected road; then taps GO and the courier walks whatever continuous path exists from start to goal, collecting coins on the way. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand drops a straight tile and a curve tile to join the hut to the flag, rotates the curve to line up, taps GO, and the courier strolls to the flag - under 10s, showing rotate and place tiles to make a road. One unscored warm-up (one straight tile bridges the gap) runs before scored layouts begin.

learning_science.principle: Spatial ability is malleable and manipulation is a core factor
learning_science.why: Rotating and placing tiles to satisfy connectivity exercises the object-manipulation spatial factor distinct from static pattern recognition.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Correct orientation of each tile is required to connect the road, so the task targets mental rotation plus placement.
learning_science.source: Uttal, D. H., et al. (2013). The malleability of spatial skills: A meta-analysis of training studies. Psychological Bulletin 139(2).

learning_science.principle: Planning as optimization over space
learning_science.why: Choosing the shortest connected route that visits coins is a spatial route-optimisation problem.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Tiles used and route length versus the optimal are scored so planful routing beats haphazard tiling.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298(1089).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (tiles and rotations versus the minimal connecting path) resists ceiling on dense boards; M-REV (re-rotations and re-placements) separates children who mentally pre-rotate each tile from guess-and-turn solvers. M-RTFIRST captures the planning pause and M-PROG turns one board into a coins-collected trajectory.
age_rationale: Tap-place-then-tap-rotate with large tiles is accessible from 2-3 on one-tile gaps. 4-5 adds curves and multiple tiles; 6-8 uses large boards with obstacles, required coin pickups and tile budgets that demand rotation foresight and route optimisation. No reading or drag precision needed.

adaptive.content_range: one-straight-tile gaps (2-3) up to large obstacle boards with curves, coins and tile budgets (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Boards are procedurally generated with a solver storing the minimal connecting-path tile count for M-EFF and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Snapping and spinning road tiles to forge a path and then watching the little courier stroll it is a cosy building hook, with fewest-tiles stars for tidy routes.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Tap-then-rotate placement removes precise-drag load; tiles are shape and pattern distinct; the full board is visible so it taxes manipulation and planning not memory; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; tile efficiency not speed is scored. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Path Coder
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_navigation: the child plans a whole route and programs a robot to walk it through a grid world to collect keys and reach the door
planning_lookahead: the full action sequence is committed before any feedback, forcing forward planning
problem_solving: find an efficient command sequence satisfying collect-keys-then-exit under a step budget
mazes_route_planning: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child lines up a sequence of move and turn arrows, then taps RUN so the robot walks the whole planned route to collect keys and reach the door.
interaction: A top-down grid shows a robot, keys, walls and a door. Below is a program strip; the child taps arrow tiles (forward, turn-left, turn-right) to append steps to the strip, taps a step to delete it, then taps RUN to execute the entire sequence at once and watch the robot move. If the robot hits a wall or misses a key they edit the program and run again. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps forward, forward, turn, forward into the strip, taps RUN, and the robot walks to the key then the door which opens - under 10s, showing build the plan then run it. One unscored warm-up (two forward steps to the door) runs before scored routes begin.

learning_science.principle: Planning measured by look-ahead before acting
learning_science.why: Committing to a whole action sequence before any feedback forces genuine forward planning rather than reactive step-by-step correction.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must queue and run a full program, so first-run success and edits-to-solve index planning quality.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298(1089).

learning_science.principle: Cognitive-map based wayfinding
learning_science.why: Sequencing turns relative to the robot's own heading requires building and transforming a spatial representation of the route.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Turn tiles are relative to the robot's facing so success reflects mental route simulation not trial taps.
learning_science.source: Tolman, E. C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review 55(4).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (program length and reruns versus the optimal sequence) is a continuous ceiling-resistant separator; first-run success and M-REV (edits before a correct run) distinguish children who mentally simulate the route from those who patch by trial. M-RTFIRST captures the planning time before the first tile and M-PROG traces keys collected across runs.
age_rationale: Tapping a few big arrow tiles then RUN is accessible from 2-3 on tiny two-step routes with no turns. 4-5 adds relative turns and one key; 6-8 uses long routes with multiple keys, forced ordering and step budgets that demand several-step look-ahead. No reading and no drag precision are needed.

adaptive.content_range: two-step no-turn routes (2-3) up to long multi-key routes with relative turns and tight step budgets (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Grids are procedurally generated with a solver storing the optimal program length for M-EFF and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Programming a robot and watching it march out your whole plan at once is a beloved coding-toy mechanic, with fewest-steps stars rewarding elegant routes.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large arrow tiles remove motor demands; the whole grid is visible so it taxes planning not memory; walls and keys are high-contrast and shape-coded; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; efficiency not speed is scored so planners who pause are rewarded. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Shape Smith
topics_techniques_covered: manipulation: the child rotates and flips puzzle pieces and places them to exactly fill a target silhouette
planning_lookahead: fitting the last piece requires ordering which piece goes where several steps ahead
problem_solving: a spatial constraint-satisfaction goal (fill the outline with no gaps or overlaps) under a move budget
spatial_visualization_construction: mentally previewing how a reoriented piece will occupy the space before placing it
form_board: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child rotates and flips a few puzzle pieces and drops them so they exactly fill the target silhouette with no gaps or overlaps.
interaction: A blank target outline sits in the middle with a tray of tangram-like pieces below. The child taps a piece to select it, taps rotate or flip buttons to orient it, then taps a spot inside the outline to place it (tap a placed piece to pick it up again). When every piece fits and the outline is fully covered the shape lights up. A move and rotation counter shows effort. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand takes a triangle, taps rotate twice, drops it into a corner of the outline, then slots a square beside it and the outline glows full - under 10s, showing turn pieces to make them fit. One unscored warm-up (two pieces into an easy outline) runs before scored silhouettes begin.

learning_science.principle: Spatial manipulation as a trainable STEM-predictive factor
learning_science.why: Mentally rotating and flipping pieces to fit a frame is the core object-transformation spatial factor.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Pieces must be reoriented before they fit, so the task isolates manipulation rather than recognition.
learning_science.source: Uttal, D. H., et al. (2013). The malleability of spatial skills: A meta-analysis of training studies. Psychological Bulletin 139(2).

learning_science.principle: Means-ends analysis in constrained assembly
learning_science.why: Fitting the last piece requires setting sub-goals about which piece goes where first, a hallmark of planful problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Pieces-over-minimum and rotation efficiency are scored so decomposing the fill is credited over blind dropping.
learning_science.source: Newell, A., & Simon, H. A. (1972). Human Problem Solving. Prentice-Hall.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (rotations and placements versus the minimal solution) is a fine continuous discriminator on hard silhouettes; M-REV separates confident pre-visualised placements from rotate-and-try. M-RTFIRST captures the pre-placement visualisation pause and M-PROG turns one hard fill into a coverage trajectory beyond solved/unsolved.
age_rationale: Tap-rotate-then-place with large pieces and snapping is accessible from 2-3 on two-piece outlines. 4-5 adds flips and three-to-four pieces; 6-8 uses many-piece silhouettes with mirror-sensitive fits and rotation budgets that demand mental transformation. No reading or precise dragging.

adaptive.content_range: two-piece easy outlines (2-3) up to many-piece mirror-sensitive silhouettes (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: need for flips versus rotations only
adaptive.notes: Silhouettes are generated from piece sets with a solver storing the minimal orientation moves for M-EFF and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: The click of a rotated piece snapping perfectly into a silhouette is deeply satisfying, and fewest-turns stars reward elegant fits.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Tap-rotate-then-place removes precise drag and rotate motor load; pieces are shape distinct; the outline is fully visible so it taxes manipulation not memory; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; move efficiency not speed is scored. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Firefly Jars
topics_techniques_covered: updating_binding: the child binds each firefly to its jar and updates that binding as the jars slide and swap positions (multiple-object tracking)
selective_filtering: distractor bugs buzz in and must be filtered from the target fireflies
attention_control: sustaining divided attention across several moving targets over the trial
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: The child watches which jars catch the glowing fireflies, keeps tracking them as the jars slide and swap places, then taps the jars that still hold a firefly.
interaction: A few fireflies fly into some jars (which briefly glow) while other jars stay empty; lids close and the jars then slide around and swap positions several times. Ordinary bugs also buzz in as distractors and must be ignored. When motion stops the child taps every jar they believe holds a firefly (tap again to deselect) then taps DONE; correct jars sparkle. Number of fireflies, swaps and distractors scales the load. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches one jar glow with a firefly, follows it as two jars swap, then taps the jar in its new spot which sparkles - under 10s, showing keep your eye on the firefly jar as they move. One unscored warm-up (one firefly, one swap) runs before scored higher-load rounds begin.

learning_science.principle: Object tracking and item-to-location binding
learning_science.why: Following target jars through motion requires continuously updating a bound representation of which object is where, taxing spatial updating and binding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Jars swap positions so the child must update bindings rather than memorise fixed locations.
learning_science.source: Pylyshyn, Z. W., & Storm, R. W. (1988). Tracking multiple independent targets: Evidence for a parallel tracking mechanism. Spatial Vision 3(3).

learning_science.principle: Executive attention and distractor resistance
learning_science.why: Ignoring buzzing distractor bugs while holding targets loads controlled attention, the driver of capacity differences.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Salient distractors must be filtered so the score reflects filtering and sustained attention not passive span.
learning_science.source: Engle, R. W. (2002). Working memory capacity as executive attention. Current Directions in Psychological Science 11(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-DPRIME distinguishes true tracking sensitivity from guessing and M-FALSEALARM counts distractor-jar taps (filtering failures). M-UPDATECOST (accuracy decrement per added swap or firefly) and M-SPAN (max fireflies tracked at criterion) give a continuous updating-capacity estimate that keeps separating high performers.
age_rationale: Watching one firefly through a single slow swap and tapping its jar is accessible from 2-3. 4-5 adds more fireflies and swaps; 6-8 uses many targets, many fast swaps and salient distractors that separate efficient trackers. Large jar tap targets and no reading keep motor and literacy load low.

adaptive.content_range: one firefly, one slow swap (2-3) up to many fireflies with many fast swaps and distractors (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Rounds are procedurally generated with firefly count staircased for M-SPAN and swaps and distractors varied for M-UPDATECOST and M-FALSEALARM.

engagement_hook: Keeping your eye on glowing fireflies as jars shuffle is a playful shell-game that pulls focused attention, and more swaps feel like a faster magic trick.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fireflies versus bugs differ by shape and animation not colour alone; large jar targets remove motor demands; swap speed is tuned per band so processing speed does not contaminate capacity; M-DPRIME corrects for guessing; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Fold-the-Net
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_visualization
paper_folding
one_liner: The child folds a flat net up into a 3D box and works out which face ends up opposite a marked face.
interaction: The child scrubs a 'fold' slider (or taps FOLD) to animate the flat net closing into a 3D cube, then drags to rotate the finished cube in 3D to inspect all faces. To answer, the child taps the color/symbol swatch that is OPPOSITE the marked star face and taps LOCK. A multiple-choice net-to-solid matching variant (pick which cube the net makes) is offered as an alternate shell.
self_teach: A ghost-hand pushes the fold slider so the net closes into a cube and spins it once; a warm-up on a simple cube with an obvious opposite face precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Surface development (net folding) is a classic spatial-visualization factor test
learning_science.why: Mentally folding a 2D net into a 3D solid is a canonical marker of the visualization factor (VZ).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an actual fold animation the child controls plus free 3D rotation, then ask for the opposite or adjacent face.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Surface Development (VZ-3).

learning_science.principle: Interactive 3D exploration supports mental-model construction better than static pictures
learning_science.why: Folding and rotating lets a child build and check an internal 3D model, especially those with weaker static imagery.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Let the child scrub the fold and orbit the cube so exploration behavior itself becomes an observable strategy signal.
learning_science.source: Hegarty (2004), Learning and Instruction 14(3):343-351, 'Dynamic visualizations and learning: getting to the difficult questions'.

tail_precision_rationale: Exploration before commit (M-EXPLORE: how much the child scrubs the fold and orbits the cube) plus error type (M-ERRTYPE: adjacent-face near-miss vs random) reveal whether a correct answer came from a solid mental model or from manipulation-by-trial; tail solvers answer hard nets (more faces, asymmetric symbols) correctly with minimal orbiting (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE), indicating internal visualization rather than externalized search.
age_rationale: Mentally mapping a 2D net to a 3D solid exceeds most K-1 children (pre-operational limits on cross-dimensional transformation), so the type starts at 2-3 with a simple six-square cube and an obvious opposite face; 4-5 adds symbols on faces; 6-8 uses irregular nets, prisms/pyramids, and adjacency (not just opposite) questions. The controllable fold animation scaffolds younger children without giving away the answer.

adaptive.content_range: simple cube net, name the opposite face (2-3) to irregular prism nets with adjacency questions and multiple candidate solids (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: net regularity; solid type (cube to prism/pyramid); symbol vs color faces; opposite vs adjacent question; number of multiple-choice candidate solids; fold-scaffold on/off
adaptive.notes: Nets are generated from valid unfoldings of a chosen solid with a fixed face-adjacency map, so the correct opposite/adjacent face is computed automatically for any clone.

engagement_hook: Watching a flat cross fold itself into a box you can spin in your hands is inherently delightful; 'origami you control'.
construct_irrelevant_risks: 3D rotation control on touch (large orbit area, momentum off); animation giving away the answer (fold stops before revealing hidden faces unless the child chooses to orbit); symbol legibility. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: X-Ray Cubes
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_visualization: infer the hidden/occluded cubes in a 3D stack and report the total number of cubes, mentally reconstructing structure that cannot be seen
spatial_visualization: reason about a cube-stack's full volume from a single viewpoint, accounting for cubes hidden behind, beneath, or supporting the visible ones
block_design: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: A pile of blocks is shown from one corner; the child works out how many blocks there are in total, including the ones hidden behind and underneath, and dials in the count.
interaction: A 3D block stack sits on a turntable the child can nudge to rotate (inspection only, logged). Because the pile is stable, some cubes must exist unseen to support the visible ones. The child sets the total-count answer on a big +/- stepper (or taps the matching numeral card) and presses DONE. An 'X-ray' button makes the stack translucent to reveal hidden cubes but is available only in the demo and warm-up; scored items disable it. No reading; the answer is a count.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand nudges a small L-stack to rotate, then taps X-ray so the pile turns glassy and a hidden cube behind the front cubes lights up while a counter ticks up; it shows that hidden blocks count too, in under 10s. One unscored warm-up on a tiny stack with a single hidden cube runs before scored items (where X-ray is off).

learning_science.principle: Spatial visualization of occluded structure
learning_science.why: Inferring cubes hidden behind or beneath visible ones separates true volumetric representation from surface feature-counting and is a canonical spatial-visualization operation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every scored stack is stable, so hidden supporting/occluded cubes are logically forced; the foil answer equals the visible-only count to catch children who ignore occlusion, and X-ray is disabled when scoring.
learning_science.source: Hegarty & Waller (2004), 'A dissociation between mental rotation and perspective-taking spatial abilities', Intelligence 32(2):175-191.

learning_science.principle: Spatial visualization as a distinct ability factor
learning_science.why: Disembedding and enumerating hidden structure loads the spatial-visualization factor, which is separable from mental rotation and strongly tied to STEM aptitude.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The task requires holding and mentally completing a 3D model rather than rotating or matching it, targeting spatial visualization specifically.
learning_science.source: Linn & Petersen (1985), 'Emergence and characterization of sex differences in spatial ability: A meta-analysis', Child Development 56(6):1479-1498.

learning_science.principle: Self-teaching via a wordless reveal demo
learning_science.why: An animated X-ray reveal makes the abstract idea that hidden cubes count concrete without instructions.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand demo flashes X-ray on/off and a warm-up trial precedes scoring, mitigating novelty-driven variance.
learning_science.source: Mayer (2005), The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-ERRTYPE is the key separator: a systematic 'visible-only' undercount means the child ignored occlusion, an off-by-one near-miss means latent ability just below the cut, and a random error means guessing - three very different tail placements a single right/wrong blurs. M-EXPLORE (how much the child rotates the stack before answering) distinguishes children who must physically inspect from those who reconstruct the hidden structure mentally, the stronger tail skill. M-RTFIRST marks the reflective encoding pause, and M-DIFFREACH escalates occlusion depth (deeper hidden layers) to pinpoint the child's volumetric-reasoning ceiling.
age_rationale: Enumerating unseen cubes requires holding a 3D model in mind, fragile in K-1 (served by concrete form-board and view types). 2-3 uses tiny stacks with at most one hidden cube and a strong support cue; 4-5 adds deeper piles with several occluded cubes; 6-8 uses tall multi-layer stacks with cubes hidden two or more layers deep and no perceptual scaffolds. Inspection-only rotation and a +/- stepper keep motor demand low.

adaptive.content_range: 3-4 cube stacks with one hidden cube (2-3) up to tall multi-layer stacks with cubes occluded two or more layers deep (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number and depth of hidden/occluded cubes
regular vs irregular (harder to infer) stacking
viewpoint that reveals more or fewer cubes
closeness of the visible-only foil to the true count
adaptive.notes: Stacks are generated on a voxel grid with a stability check so hidden supporting cubes are logically forced; the true total, the visible-only count (foil), and occlusion depth are computed exactly for M-ERRTYPE and M-DIFFREACH.

engagement_hook: Playing X-ray detective on a block pile - guessing how many blocks are really there, hidden ones and all, then (in practice) flicking on X-ray vision to watch the sneaky hidden cubes light up is a delightful reveal that rewards seeing what others miss.
construct_irrelevant_risks: X-ray reveal is available only in the demo/warm-up so scored items measure mental reconstruction, not button-pressing; inspection rotation is logged (M-EXPLORE) so it aids reasoning without becoming a motor task; keep cubes a uniform colour/shape so the task is structural not perceptual; use a coarse count range and a large stepper to limit motor and numeracy load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel hidden-count mechanic. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Plan-the-Path
topics_techniques_covered: mazes_route_planning
one_liner: The child guides a character from start to exit through a maze, and in harder items plans the shortest route that also collects required gems.
interaction: Drag the character, or tap adjacent cells / an arrow pad, to move it cell-by-cell along open corridors; walls block movement. Route-planning items require reaching the exit after collecting all gems, with a live move counter and a 'lock in route' commit for older children. The item completes when the character reaches the exit with all required gems collected.
self_teach: A ghost-hand traces the character smoothly from start through the turns to the exit; one warm-up on a tiny three-turn maze precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Route planning engages look-ahead planning (executive spatial function) beyond simple tracing
learning_science.why: Planning a multi-target shortest path taxes mental simulation of future states, a higher-order spatial component.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Add a plan-before-move, multi-gem, fewest-steps variant and score moves against the optimal path, not just completion.
learning_science.source: Shallice (1982), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298:199-209, 'Specific impairments of planning' (Tower of London paradigm).

learning_science.principle: Mazes are a long-validated child spatial/planning measure requiring foresight and impulse control
learning_science.why: Successful solving requires inhibiting the first move and planning ahead, a documented developmental spatial-executive marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Record first-move latency and dead-end entries as planning-vs-impulsive-tracing indices.
learning_science.source: Porteus (1965), 'Porteus Maze Test: Fifty Years' Application', Pacific Books.

tail_precision_rationale: First-move latency (M-RTFIRST) captures planning before acting, while path efficiency vs optimal (M-EFF) and dead-end re-entries (M-REV) reveal look-ahead depth; at the tail a long reflective pause followed by a near-optimal, backtrack-free route through a dense multi-gem maze (high M-DIFFREACH) is the plan-ahead signature that distinguishes gifted problem-solvers from fast trial-and-error tracers.
age_rationale: K-1 gets a large single-solution maze with few turns and finger-drag movement; 2-3 adds blind alleys; 4-5 introduces shortest-path with 1-2 gems; 6-8 uses dense mazes with multiple required targets and a fewest-steps budget. Wide corridors and snap-to-cell movement keep motor demand low across all bands.

adaptive.content_range: single clear path with few turns (K-1) to dense multi-gem shortest-path planning under a move budget (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; corridor branching / dead-ends; number of required gems; move budget vs optimal; plan-first (no free retrace) mode
adaptive.notes: Mazes are generated procedurally (DFS/Prim) with guaranteed solvability and a computed optimal-path length, so difficulty and the optimum for M-EFF scoring are known for every clone.

engagement_hook: A friendly character to steer, gems to grab, and 'stars for fewest steps' turn planning into a mini adventure.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (both drag and tap allowed, wide corridors); reading (none, fully wordless); rewarding speed over planning (credit efficiency and optimality, not raw time). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Which Fold Made It?
topics_techniques_covered: paper_folding
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Shown a paper before and after a single fold, the child works out which crease and direction produced the result by choosing or performing the fold.
interaction: The top shows a decorated square (before) and its folded result (after). Below are candidate fold lines (dotted) with direction arrows; the child taps the one crease-and-direction that turns the before into the after, then taps LOCK. An alternate do-it shell lets the child draw the crease by dragging between two edges and pick a direction, animating to check. Younger bands offer two or three horizontal or vertical creases; older bands add diagonal creases and off-centre folds. A REPLAY of the after-shape counts as a scaffold.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand taps a candidate crease and the before-paper folds along it into the after-shape with a chime, while a wrong crease folds to a different shape; one warm-up (two candidate creases) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Selecting the transformation that produced a result (not just predicting a result) taxes and reveals the internal fold model more fully
learning_science.why: Reasoning backward from a result to its cause is a distinct, more diagnostic demand than forward prediction (generation effect).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Make the response the fold that produced the result (an inverse task) scored against the unique crease-and-direction.
learning_science.source: Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4(6), 592-604.

learning_science.principle: Forward mental folding underlies the inverse judgment and is available in early childhood
learning_science.why: Matching a fold to its outcome relies on the same dynamic folding representation young children already possess.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep single folds and concrete before/after images so K-1 children can reason about the crease.
learning_science.source: Harris, J., Newcombe, N. S., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2013). A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: Mental paper folding in young children. Cognitive Processing, 14(2), 105-115.

tail_precision_rationale: Replay-scaffold use (M-HINT) and candidates sampled (M-EXPLORE) show whether the child infers the crease at a glance or hunts; error typing (M-ERRTYPE: correct crease line but wrong fold direction versus a wrong line) plus first-try accuracy on diagonal and off-centre folds with no replays (high M-DIFFREACH, zero M-HINT) is an inverse-folding tail signal.
age_rationale: With concrete before/after pictures and single folds, matching a fold to its result is accessible at K-1 (two candidate creases); 2-3 adds a third candidate and a direction; 4-5 adds diagonal and off-centre creases. K-1 is included because single-fold reasoning with a visible outcome is within reach; large taps keep motor demand low. It caps at 4-5 since multi-fold reversal lives in SPA-PUNCH-01 and SPA-FOLDOVER-01 at higher bands.

adaptive.content_range: two candidate creases, straight fold (K-1) to diagonal and off-centre creases with direction (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of candidate creases; crease orientation; fold direction included; off-centre folds; replay availability
adaptive.notes: The before polygon, crease, and direction determine the after polygon; distractor creases produce distinct after-shapes, so the unique key clones automatically.

engagement_hook: A reverse-engineer-the-fold puzzle: figure out the secret crease that turned the flat paper into the shape, then watch it fold to confirm.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large tappable creases); over-reliance on replay (counted via M-HINT); ambiguous folds (ensure exactly one crease-and-direction yields the after-shape); reading (icons and arrows only). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Path Connect
topics_techniques_covered: mazes_route_planning
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child rotates road or pipe tiles in a grid so a single connected path links the start to the goal, and in harder items visits required stops in the fewest tiles.
interaction: A grid is seeded with road or pipe tiles (straights, bends, T-pieces, and cross-pieces) in scrambled orientations, plus a fixed START and GOAL. The child taps a tile to rotate it 90 degrees; when the tiles form an unbroken route from start to goal the path lights up and the item completes. Route-planning items add required stop tiles that the single path must pass through, with a live tile-and-rotation counter and a fewest-tiles target for older children.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand taps a bent tile so it rotates and clicks into line, then taps one more so the road connects end to end and lights up with a chime; one unscored warm-up (a two-tile connect) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Building a connected route is a look-ahead planning and constraint-satisfaction task
learning_science.why: Forming one continuous path that satisfies connectivity (and required stops) demands mental simulation of how each tile's orientation propagates the route, a planning component of spatial problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require a single connected start-to-goal path (with required stops for harder items) and score tiles and rotations against the minimal solution rather than mere completion.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B, 298(1089), 199-209.

learning_science.principle: Orienting each tile requires mental rotation integrated with spatial visualization
learning_science.why: Judging how a bend or T-piece must be turned to accept and pass the route couples rotation with holding the whole path in mind, a core visualization demand.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use rotatable connector tiles so the child must mentally rotate each piece to see how its openings align before committing, and log rotations as a process signal.
learning_science.source: Linn, M. C., & Petersen, A. C. (1985). Emergence and characterization of sex differences in spatial ability: A meta-analysis. Child Development, 56(6), 1479-1498.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial connectivity credit (M-POLY: fraction of the route linked and required stops reached) plus rotations-versus-minimal efficiency (M-EFF) and the rotation sequence (M-PATH, M-EXPLORE) reveal whether a child sees the whole route and turns each tile purposefully or spins tiles at random (high M-REV); solving a dense grid with required stops in near-minimal rotations (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE) is the plan-the-whole-path tail signal beyond a solved or not-solved score.
age_rationale: Rotating a tile to connect two ends is accessible early, so 2-3 uses a tiny grid with a two- or three-tile straight connect; 4-5 adds bends and a longer single path; 6-8 uses a dense grid with T and cross tiles and required stops under a fewest-tiles target. Tap-to-rotate with snapping removes fine-motor demand so success reflects route planning and tile orientation rather than dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: two-to-three tile straight connect (2-3) to a dense grid of bends, T-pieces, and cross-pieces with required stops under a fewest-rotations target (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; tile mix (straights versus bends versus T and cross); number of required stops; minimal-rotation target; number of decoy tiles that must stay unused
adaptive.notes: A solvable board is generated from a known path then tiles are scrambled by random rotation, so the minimal-rotation solution and required-stop key are computed for every clone; connectivity is checked by tracing tile openings.

engagement_hook: That 'click it into line' pipe-puzzle satisfaction: tiles snap as they turn and the whole road lights up and flows when the path finally connects.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (tap-to-rotate with snap, large tiles); rotation discoverability (ghost-hand shows a tile turning); multiple valid solutions (score connectivity and rotation efficiency, accept any minimal-length connected path); rewarding blind spinning (credit M-EFF and low M-EXPLORE, not time or taps). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Fold & Punch
topics_techniques_covered: paper_folding
one_liner: The child folds a paper one or more times, punches a hole, then predicts where all the holes will be once it is unfolded.
interaction: The child taps fold controls (fold left/right, top/bottom, or a diagonal for older) to animate the sheet folding, then taps a spot to punch a hole through all layers (shown on the folded stack). The child predicts the result by tapping cells on the unfolded grid where holes will appear, then taps CHECK/LOCK. In warm-up the sheet actually unfolds to reveal the truth; in scored items the child commits predictions first.
self_teach: A ghost-hand folds the sheet once, punches, then unfolds to show the two symmetric holes; one warm-up (single fold, one punch) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Paper folding with punched holes is a benchmark spatial-visualization test
learning_science.why: Predicting the unfolded hole pattern requires mentally reversing folds and applying reflection symmetry, a core visualization operation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Have the child perform the folds and punches, then mark predicted holes on the unfolded grid as a constructed response rather than a four-option pick.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Paper Folding (VZ-2).

learning_science.principle: A single wordless worked demonstration teaches a novel spatial rule faster than instructions (worked-example effect)
learning_science.why: Worked examples reduce cognitive load for novices, so the unfold-reveal teaches the reflection rule without text.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The warm-up performs one full fold-punch-unfold as a wordless worked example, then scored items withhold the reveal until after commit.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (1998), Educational Psychology Review 10(3):251-296, 'Cognitive architecture and instructional design' (worked-example effect).

tail_precision_rationale: Scoring predicted-vs-true holes as graded overlap (M-POLY) and classifying misses (M-ERRTYPE: correct hole count but wrong reflection axis is a systematic near-miss vs random) extracts fine tail information from one item; the sharpest separator is accuracy on multi-fold, asymmetric-punch items (high M-DIFFREACH) where each extra fold doubles the required reflections, so able children track all layers while others lose a fold.
age_rationale: Reversing folds by reflection is beyond most K-1 children, so the type begins at 2-3 with a single fold and one punch on a coarse grid; 4-5 uses two orthogonal folds; 6-8 uses three folds including an oblique fold and multiple punches. Tapping large grid cells keeps motor demand minimal, and the live unfold in warm-up scaffolds the rule.

adaptive.content_range: single fold plus one punch on a 4x4 grid (2-3) to three folds including an oblique fold with multiple punches on a fine grid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of folds; fold orientation (orthogonal vs oblique); number and position of punches; grid resolution; symmetric vs asymmetric layout
adaptive.notes: A fold sequence plus punch coordinates define the item; the true unfolded hole set is computed by reflecting punches across each fold axis in reverse order, so every clone is auto-keyed and partial credit is exact.

engagement_hook: Hands-on 'fold the paper, punch it, guess the surprise' with a satisfying unfold reveal; like a magic trick the child performs.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large grid taps); giving away the rule (reveal only in warm-up or after commit); grid-resolution ambiguity (snap punches to cell centers). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Rolling Cube
topics_techniques_covered: mental_rotation: track the changing orientation of a marked cube as it tips 90 degrees from square to square along a path (sequential rotation)
spatial_visualization: predict which face (symbol) ends up on top or facing a given direction after a series of rolls
mental_rotation: apply successive turns and integrate them into a final orientation rather than judging a single rotation
spatial_visualization: reason about the fixed adjacency of cube faces under rolling
one_liner: A cube with a picture on each face tips over square by square along a path, and the child works out which picture ends up on top when it stops.
interaction: A cube with distinct symbols on its faces sits on the start of a short arrow path of squares. The child taps PLAY to watch it tip/roll 90 degrees to each next square (or steps it one roll at a time with a step button). At the end the child answers by tapping which symbol is now on top (from a set of face options), or in a variant rolls a response cube to show the final orientation. The roll animation can be replayed; only the final answer is keyed. Step-by-step mode logs partial tracking.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps PLAY and the cube tips once, pausing so the child sees the top face change to the face that was in front; a small top-face badge updates with each tip. The warm-up is a single roll where the answer is directly seen, teaching that rolling swaps top and side faces before any multi-roll scoring.

learning_science.principle: Sequential mental rotation and orientation updating
learning_science.why: Integrating successive 90-degree rotations into a final orientation is a chronometric spatial operation that loads spatial working memory beyond a single rotation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty scales with the number of rolls and turns, requiring the child to update and maintain orientation across steps rather than judge one transform.
learning_science.source: Shepard & Metzler (1971), Science 171(3972)

learning_science.principle: Mental animation of a moving object
learning_science.why: Predicting the outcome of a dynamic process (rolling) indexes the ability to run a mental simulation, a strong spatial-reasoning marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must simulate the roll internally to answer in one-shot mode; the step mode reveals whether they can chunk the simulation.
learning_science.source: Hegarty (1992), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 18(5)

learning_science.principle: Fixed face-adjacency constraint learning
learning_science.why: Understanding that opposite faces stay opposite under rolling is a spatial invariant that supports efficient tracking.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Face layouts are consistent within an item so a child can exploit adjacency structure, and errors reveal who has not internalized the invariant.
learning_science.source: Piaget & Inhelder (1956), The Child's Conception of Space

tail_precision_rationale: M-PROG (accuracy of the child's intermediate top-face reads in step mode) turns one rolling item into an orientation-tracking curve, showing whether errors accumulate gradually (drift) or appear suddenly (a specific mis-roll), which sharpens tail placement beyond a final bit. M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a single-axis confusion (rolled the wrong way once) from a lost-track scramble, and M-DIFFREACH escalates the number of rolls and turn directions to locate the child's tracking ceiling. M-PATH logs the replays and step usage as a strategy signature, and M-RTFIRST indexes pre-answer mental simulation.
age_rationale: Tracking orientation across multiple tips overloads K-1 (served by the single-turn rotation and match types); a single roll can suit late K-1 but the type is scored from 2-3 up. 2-3 uses 1-2 straight rolls; 4-5 uses 3-4 rolls with one turn; 6-8 uses longer paths with multiple turns and one-shot (no step) mode. Answering is a single tap; the roll is automated so no fine motor control is needed.

adaptive.content_range: 1-2 straight rolls answered in step mode (grades 2-3) up to long multi-turn paths simulated one-shot (6-8)
difficulty_levers: number and direction of turns in the path
step mode (partial tracking) vs one-shot simulation
target face queried (top vs a named side)
adaptive.notes: Paths and cube labelings are generated with the final orientation computed by exact rotation composition, so the key, per-step top faces, and plausible foils are automatic; clones at high throughput.

engagement_hook: A tumbling-dice adventure - watch the cube flip along its trail and call which picture lands face-up; being right about a long roll feels like a magic trick.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Automate the roll so no dexterity is needed and the construct is spatial tracking, not motor control; allow replays without penalty (logged) so attention lapses are not misread; use distinct, culturally neutral face symbols and pair with color so symbols are discriminable; step mode offloads memory to isolate rotation from span; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel rolling mechanic. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: What the Robot Sees
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
spatial_visualization
one_liner: A robot sits at one side of a little scene; the child rebuilds what the robot sees by ordering the objects left-to-right from the robot's point of view.
interaction: A scene of a few distinct objects is shown from above with a robot token on one side. The child reconstructs the robot's view by dragging object cards into a 'what the robot sees' strip in the correct left-to-right order (and, for older bands, marking which object looks nearest). Dragging the robot to a new side updates nothing automatically in scored items, so the child must imagine the view. The child taps LOCK to submit the ordered strip; partial credit is given for correctly ordered pairs.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand walks the robot to a side and then slots the object cards into the strip in the order the robot sees them, flipping left-and-right versus the top-down map; one warm-up (two objects) with a live-updating strip precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Level-2 perspective taking (how a scene looks from another viewpoint) is a distinct developmental milestone
learning_science.why: Beyond knowing what another can see, reconstructing how objects are arranged from someone else's viewpoint requires a genuine viewpoint transformation that emerges in childhood.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Have the child produce the seen left-to-right ordering from the robot's viewpoint, isolating appearance/arrangement (Level-2) rather than mere visibility (Level-1).
learning_science.source: Masangkay, McCluskey, McIntyre, Sims-Knight, Vaughn & Flavell (1974), Child Development 45(2):357-366, 'The early development of inferences about the visual percepts of others'.

learning_science.principle: Concrete, movable scenes scaffold the viewpoint shift and reduce egocentric error
learning_science.why: Young children default to their own view; a movable robot and draggable cards let them build the other viewpoint concretely instead of holding it purely in imagery.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a live-updating strip in warm-up and discrete viewpoints, then withhold the live update in scored items so the ordering must be imagined.
learning_science.source: Newcombe & Huttenlocher (1992), Developmental Psychology 28(4):635-643, 'Children's early ability to solve perspective-taking problems'.

tail_precision_rationale: Scoring the produced ordering as correctly ordered pairs (M-POLY) and typing errors (M-ERRTYPE: a clean left-right reversal is an egocentric near-miss versus a scrambled random order) grades perspective responses far more finely than right/wrong; at the tail, correct orderings from opposite and side viewpoints (large offsets) with little card-shuffling (low M-EXPLORE, high M-DIFFREACH) mark a true allocentric model rather than reading off the child's own view.
age_rationale: Robust other-viewpoint reconstruction emerges around ages 6-8, so the type starts at 2-3 with two objects and a live-updating strip (recognition support); 4-5 uses three objects and side viewpoints; 6-8 uses four or more objects, opposite and diagonal viewpoints, and a near/far judgment. Draggable cards give concrete support so younger children are not blocked by pure imagery, and K-1 is excluded because egocentric responding dominates.

adaptive.content_range: order two objects from a side view with a live strip (2-3) to order four or more objects from an opposite or diagonal viewpoint with a near/far mark (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; viewpoint offset (same side, side, opposite, diagonal); live-updating strip on or off; near/far depth judgment included; object distinctiveness
adaptive.notes: Objects are placed at coordinates and the correct seen ordering from any viewpoint is computed geometrically by projecting onto the robot's left-right axis, so items and keys clone automatically; works_well is medium because the construct's onset is late and floor effects appear before about age 6.

engagement_hook: Become a director seeing through a robot's eyes: walk it around the set and rebuild its shot, with cards clicking into a filmstrip of what it sees.
