construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor for young bands (report reliability, exclude K-1); reading (objects are icons, not words); motor (draggable cards with snap slots); mistaking a consistent left-right reversal for random error (type egocentric reversals separately); over-support (live strip only in warm-up). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Shadow Play
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_visualization: predict the 2D shadow (silhouette) a 3D object casts from a given light direction (projection to an outline)
spatial_visualization: match a solid to the shadow it makes, or rotate the solid so its shadow matches a target outline
spatial_visualization: distinguish which features of a solid survive as outline vs collapse under projection
cross_sections: contrast an outline projection with an internal slice (the shadow is the silhouette, not a cut face)
perspective_taking: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: A light shines on a 3D object and the child works out the flat shadow it throws on the wall - or turns the object until its shadow matches a target.
interaction: A 3D object (cup, cone, arch, L-solid) sits between a light (a sun/lamp icon showing the direction) and a screen. The child either taps which of several 2D silhouettes is the shadow cast in that direction, or drags to rotate the object and taps LOCK when its live-projected shadow matches a shown target outline. A ghosted shadow can be previewed by tapping a light-toggle (exploration). The keyed silhouette (or an orientation within tolerance) is scored.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps the light-toggle and a faint shadow appears on the screen; it points from the object along the light rays to the matching silhouette, which lights up. In the rotate variant it spins the object a little and the live shadow morphs, then taps LOCK when it matches. The warm-up uses a ball (whose shadow is a circle from any side) so the projection idea lands wordlessly.

learning_science.principle: Projective spatial concepts
learning_science.why: Coordinating how a solid looks as a projected outline is a projective-space concept that develops distinctly from Euclidean/rotation reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must reason about projection (which features become the outline from a given direction), a transformation absent from the catalog's rotation, folding, and section types.
learning_science.source: Piaget & Inhelder (1956), The Child's Conception of Space

learning_science.principle: Spatial visualization of surface-to-outline mapping
learning_science.why: Deciding which 3D features survive as silhouette and which collapse indexes robust spatial visualization.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Objects are chosen so the correct shadow depends on the light direction (a cup is a rectangle from the side but a ring/disk from the top), forcing direction-specific projection.
learning_science.source: Linn & Petersen (1985), Child Development 56(6)

learning_science.principle: Learning by exploratory manipulation
learning_science.why: Letting the child preview the live shadow supports hypothesis testing and self-teaches the projection mapping.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A light-toggle preview and (in the rotate variant) a live shadow give immediate spatial feedback; M-EXPLORE logs how much preview was used.
learning_science.source: Sodian, Zaitchik & Carey (1991), Child Development 62(4)

tail_precision_rationale: M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a wrong-direction error (child projected the object from the wrong side) from a feature-collapse error (kept a feature that the projection removes), pinpointing the specific projective misconception near the cut. M-EXPLORE (use of the shadow preview) separates children who must empirically test from those who project mentally, a coach-resistant strategy signal, and M-DIFFREACH escalates object complexity and asymmetry (from a sphere to an asymmetric L-solid whose three shadows all differ) to find the ceiling. M-CONF on a subset down-weights lucky picks and M-RTFIRST indexes pre-answer projection.
age_rationale: Shadow matching is concrete and intuitive from K-1 (a ball makes a round shadow), so the type spans all bands. K-1 uses simple objects and one light direction with a select-the-shadow response; 2-3 and 4-5 add direction-dependent objects (cup, cone); 6-8 uses asymmetric solids where all three principal shadows differ and adds the rotate-to-match variant. Tap-to-select keeps motor demand minimal for the youngest; rotation is reserved for older bands.

adaptive.content_range: simple object, one light direction, select-the-shadow (K-1) up to asymmetric solids with direction-dependent shadows and rotate-to-match (6-8)
difficulty_levers: light direction and whether it is stated or must be inferred
how similar the silhouette foils are
adaptive.notes: Objects are parametric solids whose true silhouette from any direction is rendered/computed exactly, so keyed shadows and near-miss foils are generated automatically; clones at high throughput.

engagement_hook: A shadow-puppet game - shine the light and guess the shape on the wall, or twist the object until its shadow snaps onto the target; the reveal of the true shadow is delightful.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ensure the correct shadow is genuinely direction-dependent (not guessable from the object's most familiar view) so the construct is projection; make silhouette foils differ by geometry, not shading; keep objects culturally neutral and recognizable; the light preview is logged (M-EXPLORE) so it informs without becoming a motor task; reserve rotate-to-match for older bands to limit motor load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls the novel projection mechanic. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Shape-Fill Form Board
topics_techniques_covered: form_board
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child drags loose puzzle pieces, rotating them when needed, to completely fill a target silhouette.
interaction: Drag each piece from the tray into the outline; a piece snaps into place when it is close and correctly oriented. A selected piece is rotated with a rotate handle or tap (snaps 45 degrees) and flipped for older bands. The item auto-submits when the silhouette is fully covered, or the child taps DONE; partial fills are scored by the fraction of area correctly placed.
self_teach: A ghost-hand drags one piece into the outline and it snaps with a click; a two-piece warm-up requiring no rotation precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Spatial assembly ('form board') is a distinct, strong marker of the visualization factor
learning_science.why: Composing parts into a whole taps figure-ground segmentation and mental transformation beyond simple perception.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use loose draggable pieces that fill a silhouette (a digital form board) rather than a 'which pieces fit' multiple-choice picture.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Manual for Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Form Board (VZ) marker tests.

learning_science.principle: Manipulatives externalize spatial reasoning and reduce working-memory load
learning_science.why: Physically moving pieces lets a child test partial solutions instead of holding them in mind, widening who can demonstrate the skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Allow free rearrangement and undo with snap-to slots so exploration is cheap and only strategy, not memory, is taxed.
learning_science.source: Newcombe (2010), American Educator 34(2):29-35, 'Picture this: increasing math and science learning by improving spatial thinking'.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial-area credit (M-POLY) plus placement efficiency (M-EFF: pieces placed vs re-dragged) and the placement sequence (M-PATH) turn one silhouette into a rich curve; strong solvers place large anchor pieces first and finish with few re-drags, so near-optimal assembly of a hard multi-piece silhouette at speed separates the tail even when several children all reach full coverage.
age_rationale: K-1 gets 2-3 large pieces, no rotation required, and a generous snap radius; 2-3 needs simple 90-degree rotations; 4-5 adds 45-degree rotations and more pieces; 6-8 uses 6-9 tangram pieces requiring rotation and reflection. Fine placement is removed by snapping so success reflects visualization rather than dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: 2-piece slide-together (K-1) to 9-piece rotate-and-reflect tangram silhouettes (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: piece count; rotation/reflection required; snap radius; silhouette ambiguity (multiple valid tilings); interior guide lines on/off
adaptive.notes: Silhouettes and piece sets are generated from a tiling engine, with difficulty set by number of pieces and required transformations; any complete tiling is accepted.

engagement_hook: Classic tangram/puzzle satisfaction: pieces click home and the silhouette lights up when complete, with a 'perfect fit' streak.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor drag precision (snap-to); rotation-control discoverability (ghost-hand shows the rotate handle); silhouettes with multiple valid solutions (accept any complete tiling, score coverage not one key). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: What Do They See
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
one_liner: The child figures out what a character sees from where it stands, by moving the character or pointing a dial toward a target from the character's viewpoint.
interaction: A small scene of labeled objects is shown from above with a character token. As the child drags the character around the scene (snapping to set viewpoints), a live 'what they see' strip updates, showing the objects in the character's left-to-right order. To answer, the child either drags the character to the spot that would produce a shown view, or (older bands) rotates a pointer dial to indicate the direction to a hidden target as seen from the character's heading, then taps LOCK.
self_teach: A ghost-hand walks the character to the other side and the 'what they see' strip flips left-to-right; a warm-up asks the child to match one simple two-object view before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Perspective taking (spatial orientation) is a spatial factor dissociable from object rotation
learning_science.why: Imagining a scene from another viewpoint (self-to-object) is separable from mentally rotating objects and predicts navigation ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score directional/heading error to a target from an imagined viewpoint, not object rotation, to isolate the perspective factor.
learning_science.source: Kozhevnikov & Hegarty (2001), Memory & Cognition 29(5):745-756, 'A dissociation between object manipulation spatial ability and spatial orientation ability'.

learning_science.principle: Young children default to their own view (egocentrism) and improve with concrete, movable viewpoints
learning_science.why: The three-mountains work shows perspective taking develops later, and letting children move a character scaffolds the viewpoint shift.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a live, movable character and start with 2-4 discrete viewpoints for younger bands rather than abstract heading estimation.
learning_science.source: Piaget & Inhelder (1956), 'The Child's Conception of Space' (three-mountains task), Routledge & Kegan Paul.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Perspective-taking angular error
new_measurements_proposed.what: Signed angular error between the child's indicated heading/direction and the true direction to the target from an imagined viewpoint.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Grades perspective responses far more finely than right/wrong, and its systematic component quantifies residual egocentric bias; low angular error at large viewpoint offsets is a navigation-linked tail signal standard batteries omit.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: On pointing/heading items, record the dial angle and subtract the geometric correct heading; decompose into random and egocentric-bias components.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=10 pointing trials across a range of viewpoint offsets for a stable error and bias estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: Continuous heading/pointing error (M-VIEWANG) grades responses far more finely than right/wrong, and its systematic component (pointing as if from the child's own position) quantifies residual egocentric bias; at the tail, low angular error on large viewpoint offsets (>=135 degrees) with little exploration (M-EXPLORE) marks children with a true allocentric model, a navigation-linked spatial strength standard batteries omit.
age_rationale: Robust allocentric perspective taking emerges around ages 6-8, so the type starts at 2-3 with only 2-4 discrete viewpoints and a live-updating view strip (recognition, not generation); 4-5 uses more objects and 4-8 viewpoints; 6-8 uses continuous pointing-dial heading estimation. The movable character gives concrete support so younger children are not blocked by pure imagery, and K-1 is excluded because egocentric responding dominates.

adaptive.content_range: match a two-object view among 2-4 viewpoints (2-3) to continuous dial heading toward a target from an imagined orientation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; number and spacing of viewpoints; discrete match vs continuous pointing; viewpoint offset magnitude; self vs array reference frame
adaptive.notes: Scenes are generated by placing N labeled objects at coordinates and the correct view/heading is computed geometrically, so items and keys clone automatically; works_well is 'med' because the construct's onset is late and floor effects appear before about age 6.

engagement_hook: A character with a live 'camera view' you control: move it around and watch the world reorder from its eyes; it feels like directing a scene.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor for young bands (report reliability, exclude K-1); reading (labels replaced by icons); motor (snap viewpoints, coarse dial detents for younger); mistaking left/right mirroring for error (score angular direction consistently). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Place the Slice
topics_techniques_covered: cross_sections
spatial_visualization
one_liner: Given the exact 2D shape wanted, the child positions and tilts a cutting plane through a 3D solid so the cut face becomes that shape.
interaction: A target 2D shape (for example a hexagon or an oval) is shown. The child drags a height slider to move a cutting plane up and down through a rotatable solid and, for older bands, drags a tilt handle to angle it; a live outline previews the current cut face. When the previewed cut matches the target the child taps LOCK. Partial credit is given for how closely the produced cross-section matches the target. An alternate 'build the cut' shell has the child place vertices to draw the resulting cross-section polygon.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand tilts the plane through a cube until the preview outline morphs into the shown hexagon and snaps green; one unscored warm-up (make a square from a straight cut of a cube) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Cross-sectioning (penetrative thinking) is a trainable STEM-linked spatial skill
learning_science.why: Inferring how a plane meets a solid underlies geology, anatomy, and engineering and is separable from other spatial factors.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an interactive plane whose height and tilt the child controls, and require producing a named cross-section rather than only recognizing one.
learning_science.source: Cohen & Hegarty (2012), Learning and Individual Differences 22(6):868-874, 'Inferring cross sections: when internal visualizations are more important than properties of external visualizations'.

learning_science.principle: Generating a solution produces stronger, more diagnostic performance than recognizing one (generation effect)
learning_science.why: Requiring the child to construct the cut plane, rather than pick from options, taxes and reveals the internal model more fully and resists guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Make the response an inverse construction (set the plane to hit a target shape) scored by continuous match, not a four-option choice.
learning_science.source: Slamecka & Graf (1978), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory 4(6):592-604, 'The generation effect: delineation of a phenomenon'.

tail_precision_rationale: Continuous match of the produced cross-section (M-POLY) plus plane-adjustment efficiency (M-EFF) and exploration before commit (M-EXPLORE) turn one inverse item into a graded curve; the tail signal is producing a hard oblique cross-section (a hexagon from a cube, an ellipse from a cone) with few plane moves and near-zero placement error (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE), evidence of an internal penetrative model rather than scrub-until-it-looks-right search.
age_rationale: Predicting and producing internal cross-sections is difficult before about age 9 and keeps improving through adolescence, so the type is scoped to 4-5 (familiar solids, straight axis-aligned targets like circle and square, tilt disabled) and 6-8 (prisms, cones, pyramids with oblique targets like ellipse, rectangle, and hexagon, tilt enabled). It is excluded from K-1 and 2-3 because penetrative thinking is largely undeveloped and would floor.

adaptive.content_range: make a circle or square with a straight cut of a familiar solid (4-5) to make a hexagon or ellipse with an oblique cut of a prism, cone, or pyramid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: target-shape difficulty; solid type; tilt enabled or disabled; match tolerance; number of plane degrees of freedom; distance from the obvious axis-aligned cut
adaptive.notes: For a library of solids the set of achievable cross-sections and the plane parameters that yield each are precomputed, so target shapes and their keyed plane placements clone automatically; oblique and irregular solids need more authoring, hence medium cloneability.

engagement_hook: A 'carve it to order' puzzle: you are handed the shape you must reveal, then tilt and slide the knife through the solid until the hidden face pops out exactly right.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (scoped to 4-5 and up); 3D rendering legibility (clear edges, controllable rotation); plane-control discoverability (ghost-hand demo); rewarding blind scrubbing (credit efficiency M-EFF and low exploration, not time); match tolerance tuned so a rough placement does not score as exact. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Scan Stacker
topics_techniques_covered: cross_sections
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child scrubs through a stack of 2D cross-section slices (like a medical scan) and works out which 3D solid would produce them.
interaction: A slider scrubs a scan line from the top of a hidden solid to the bottom, showing the 2D cross-section at each height as a stack of slices the child can replay. To answer, the child taps which of several candidate 3D solids would produce that exact sequence of cross-sections and taps LOCK; an alternate 'build it' shell has the child stack sized disks or plates to assemble the solid the slices imply. Distractor solids differ in how a single slice would change (for example a cone versus a cylinder versus a pyramid).
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand scrubs the scan of a cone so the circle slice shrinks from big to a point, then taps the cone among the candidates with a green chime; one unscored warm-up (a cylinder whose circle stays the same size) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Cross-sectioning (penetrative thinking) is a STEM-linked spatial skill
learning_science.why: Relating a solid to its internal planar cross-sections underlies geology, anatomy, and engineering and is separable from other spatial factors.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present the full sequence of cross-sections and require inferring the solid, so the child reasons about how the cut face changes with height rather than reading one static picture.
learning_science.source: Cohen, C. A., & Hegarty, M. (2012). Inferring cross sections: When internal visualizations are more important than properties of external visualizations. Learning and Individual Differences, 22(6), 868-874.

learning_science.principle: Integrating a series of slices into a whole is section-to-3D mental synthesis
learning_science.why: Building a 3D model from successive cross-sections is exactly the skill experts use to read medical and geological scans, and it predicts and is supported by spatial training.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Have the child scrub and replay the slice stack and then identify or assemble the implied solid, logging how much scrubbing precedes the commit.
learning_science.source: Hegarty, M., Keehner, M., Khooshabeh, P., & Montello, D. R. (2009). How spatial abilities enhance, and are enhanced by, dental education. Learning and Individual Differences, 19(1), 61-70.

tail_precision_rationale: How much the child scrubs and replays the stack before committing (M-EXPLORE) and near-miss typing (M-ERRTYPE: choosing a cylinder for a cone reads the first slice but not the change, versus a random pick) reveal whether the solid is inferred from the slice progression or guessed from one frame; correctly identifying or assembling hard solids (cones, pyramids, composite shapes) with little scrubbing (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE) marks an internal section-to-3D model, and the build shell adds graded assembly credit (M-POLY).
age_rationale: Penetrative, section-to-solid reasoning largely develops after about age 9 and keeps improving through adolescence, so the type is scoped to 4-5 (familiar solids with clearly changing slices such as a cone versus a cylinder, few candidates) and 6-8 (prisms, pyramids, and composite solids with subtly changing slices and close distractors). K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because the skill is largely undeveloped and would floor. Slider scrubbing and tap-to-pick keep motor demand minimal.

adaptive.content_range: pick among a cone, cylinder, and sphere from clearly changing slices (4-5) to identify or stack-build prisms, pyramids, and composite solids from subtly changing slices (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: solid set and similarity of candidates; how much the slice changes with height; number of candidates; identify versus build-by-stacking response; presence of a composite two-part solid
adaptive.notes: For a library of solids the height-indexed cross-section sequence is precomputed, so slice stacks and keys clone automatically; composite and irregular solids need more authoring, hence medium cloneability.

engagement_hook: Play scan-room detective: scrub a glowing scan up and down through a mystery object and watch the slice morph, then call out what solid is hiding inside.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (scoped to 4-5 and up, report reliability); slice legibility (clear high-contrast slices, replayable stack); slider discoverability (ghost-hand demonstrates scrubbing); distractor similarity tuned so one-frame guessing is penalized (M-ERRTYPE); device screen size for candidate solids (large tappable candidates). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Transform Machine
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_transformation: six hidden transformations of a block figure on a 4x4 lattice, each standing behind an arbitrary badge under a per-block mapping; the child induces what each badge does from the machine’s visible outcomes, because no badge is ever explained

visual_rule_discovery: infer a small closed vocabulary of lattice moves and then the fact that they COMPOSE in the order shown, which is the deep half of the system and the half that only appears on chains of two or more

mental_rotation: one of the six transformations is a quarter turn and a second is a reflection, so re-orientation is part of the vocabulary — but a deliberate minority of it, and never required, because chains using no orientation badge exist at every rung
figure_classification: five candidate figures, every one of them the output of some incomplete version of the system, so no option can be dismissed as an obvious non-answer

sequential_transformation: composition depth is the ladder, from one transformation to three, and figure density is the second ladder that carries the top of the difficulty scale without deepening the chain
one_liner: A machine shows the badges it is about to use, in order, then rearranges a small pattern of blocks; the child works out what each badge does by watching the machine work, then taps the pattern it will make.
interaction: A row of one to three badges shows the transformations the machine will apply, in order, to a pattern of blocks on a 4x4 lattice. The child taps which of five output patterns the machine produces. ONE TAP, five options in fixed positions, no drag and no construction — deliberately the same response grammar as SPA-ROLL-01, SPA-FOLDNET-01 and SPA-SHADOW-01, all three of which are S1 spatial types already wired and served, so the interface load is discharged in Stage 1 instead of landing inside the scored block where it would be indistinguishable from learning. Before the first scored trial an UNSCORED interface gate runs depth-0 instances, where the machine applies no badge at all so the answer is visible, to a criterion of k consecutive correct; a child who has not got the interface never reaches trial 0. Gate instances are produced by the renderer and are not bank items. After the child commits, the machine completes its action and the correct pattern simply becomes the next visible state: informational feedback only, with no verdict, score, streak, praise, points or performance-contingent animation anywhere. The reveal is supplied by the host AFTER the server has scored the trial — the renderer never holds the correct pattern, because the badge-to-transformation mapping is server-only and must not reach the browser. RENDERER CONSTRAINT, RECORDED HERE BECAUSE IT IS A SPEC-TIME DECISION AND NOT A U6 DETAIL: the lattice is drawn as faint dots and never as a ruled or boxed table, and no badge or block ever carries a border, frame, halo or outline. A blind audit of FLU-OPCHAIN-01 found its `ring` transformation drawn as a rounded rectangle indistinguishable from a UI border, with children inducing over the furniture rather than over the figure; this type closes that structurally, because every transformation in its vocabulary is a permutation of the lattice cells and therefore cannot add, remove or enclose anything.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps one of the five outputs on a depth-0 instance where the machine applies no badge, so the pattern comes out unchanged and the tap-one-of-five loop is obvious wordlessly. The machine then runs worked single-badge instances in front of the child, which fade on a FIXED schedule rather than a performance-contingent one: a fading schedule that responded to performance would make trial index mean something different for each child and the fitted climb would stop being comparable, which is the only property it currently has.

learning_science.principle: Induction of a hidden system, not trained rotation — the load-bearing framing choice
learning_science.why: Spatial skill is trainable (g = 0.47 across 206 studies) and within-session mental-rotation improvement is well enough documented to be treated as a confound, so a spatial block built as "rotate these, faster and better" is close to guaranteed to produce a positive rate for everyone — indistinguishable from the 0.33 SD retest artifact the field’s own meta-analysis reports on a second administration. A design that cannot fail to show a climb is not measuring learning rate; it is measuring warm-up.
learning_science.concrete_decision: What is learnable is WHICH transformation each badge stands for, not how well the child executes it. Four of the six transformations are rearrangements no amount of rotation skill performs; the orientation count is a free difficulty lever whose value 0 is reachable at every depth, so 36% of the bank requires no re-orientation at all and no rung of the ladder requires one. At least four of the five options on every item are patterns SOME badge relabelling produces, so a solver with perfect spatial execution and no knowledge of the mapping is held at 1-in-4 against a 1-in-5 baseline. Scoring is accuracy only and response time never enters the fitted rate, because rotation latency is exactly the quantity that improves with practice.
learning_science.source: Uttal et al. (2013), Psychological Bulletin 139(2); Scharfen, Peters & Holling (2018), Intelligence 67, 44-66; Jost (2021), dissertation, University of Regensburg (T3, unrefereed, cited for the methodological point only)

learning_science.principle: Graded induction over a composable vocabulary, not single-rule insight
learning_science.why: A one-rule discovery task produces a step function — chance until insight, then near-ceiling — and fitting a linear rate to a step recovers only roughly when the step arrived, wasting most of the trials. A closed vocabulary whose primitives compose makes "having learned it" a ladder rather than a switch.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Six transformations, composition depth 1 to 3, so the adaptive target has somewhere to go after the first insight and the rate summarises successive abstraction rather than the timing of one event. Chains whose composed permutation is reachable by a shorter chain are rejected, so a stated depth is always an honest depth.
learning_science.source: Harlow (1949) learning set; Estes (1956) on group vs individual curve form

learning_science.principle: Transfer across items, because no item may repeat
learning_science.why: The block forbids repeats, since a re-served item measures recall of that item. So whatever is learned has to transfer between items, which rules out teaching and testing the same instance and leaves a hidden generative system as the only workable shape.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The badge-to-transformation mapping persists across the whole block while every trial is a fresh pattern; the system is what carries forward, never the item.
learning_science.source: Lionello-DeNolf, McIlvane, Canovas, de Souza & Barros (2008), The Psychological Record 58(1)

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load — extraneous interface load vs germane induction
learning_science.why: A climb produced by a child working out where to tap is indistinguishable, inside the fit, from a climb produced by learning the system. Together with rotation practice that is the most likely way this type fails.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Response grammar reused verbatim from three S1 spatial types every child meets during spatial bracketing; single tap; fixed option positions so position-search is not itself learnable; an unscored interface gate to criterion before trial 0.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (2019), Educational Psychology Review 31(2); Mayer (2021), Multimedia Learning 3rd ed.

learning_science.principle: Retrieval practice with informational, non-evaluative feedback
learning_science.why: A learning block with no feedback has nothing to learn from, but evaluative feedback degrades performance in about a third of studies and leaks into the ability estimate; 8-9-year-olds also lose more from negative feedback than adults do, which would make an error-driven design partly a measure of tolerance for being told you are wrong, differentially by age.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The answer is never revealed before the child commits; the reveal is the machine’s completed action, shown as a state rather than a verdict, with no error salience and no error count.
learning_science.source: Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Psychological Science 17(3); Kluger & DeNisi (1996), Psychological Bulletin 119(2); van Duijvenvoorde et al. (2008), Journal of Neuroscience 28(38)

learning_science.principle: No multi-dimensional integration at the young bands, on BOTH dimensions
learning_science.why: A wrong difficulty ordering biases the fitted rate rather than merely adding noise, and 6-7-year-olds were mostly best fit by a random-response model on an information-integration structure. This design has two dimensions a young child could be floored by, not one: how many transformations compose, and how many blocks must be tracked through them.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Both are capped by grade band. Composition depth: 1 at K-1, 2 at 2-3 and 4-5, 3 at 6-8. Figure density: 4 blocks at K-1, 5 at 2-3, 6 at 4-5, 7 at 6-8. Both caps are checkable from the item’s own levers.
learning_science.source: Nosofsky & Palmeri (1996), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 3(2); Li, Huang, Seger & Liu (2024), British Journal of Developmental Psychology 42(4)

learning_science.principle: Desirable difficulty, and why it belongs only in Stage 2
learning_science.why: Aiming above the child’s settled standing depresses current performance, which is exactly why it must not leak back into the standing estimate; inside a block whose job is to observe a climb it is the mechanism rather than a slogan.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The block targets standing + 1 and follows the child up as the fit projects a climb; the bank therefore carries 0.5-point grain across the whole 1-20 scale so the target always has an item to land on, and the top of that scale is reached by figure density rather than by chain depth so the pool does not thin out for the fastest climbers.
learning_science.source: Bjork & Bjork (2011); Soderstrom & Bjork (2015), Perspectives on Psychological Science 10(2)

tail_precision_rationale: The headline quantity is M-LEARNRATE fitted over the 30-trial block. M-RTFIRST is recorded as a DIAGNOSTIC only and never enters the fit: response time on a spatial task falls with practice for everyone, so admitting it would import the exact contamination this design exists to exclude, and a rate correlating with opening-trial latency is evidence of interface learning rather than of induction. The second quantity is a per-trial STRATEGY TRACE, and it is not a nicety: every distractor encodes one named incomplete version of the system (two badges applied in the wrong order, a badge re-oriented the other way, a badge applied twice, a badge read as a different transformation, a badge skipped, two badges read as a different pair, only the first badge applied, no badge applied), so each response is classifiable against a closed rule set, and every slate names at least two distinct failures so migration between them is observable. That gives a falsification test the rate alone cannot give — in a real learner errors should migrate from spread-out toward misread-badge and wrong-order — and it gives an ORDINAL fallback if the rate turns out real but too small to report. The trace is carried on answer.strategyTrace and on each option’s distractorRationales entry, and is counted through the existing M-ERRTYPE and M-RULEID; no new measurement is proposed here.
age_rationale: Two caps by band rather than one, because this design has two dimensions the developmental evidence constrains. Composition depth is the dimensionality of the rule: 1 at K-1 (difficulty 1-4), 2 at 2-3 (4-8) and at 4-5 (8-12), 3 at 6-8 (12-20). Figure density is how many blocks must be tracked through it: 4 at K-1, 5 at 2-3, 6 at 4-5, 7 at 6-8. The cap at the young end is not caution about difficulty but about a floor that would misread as low ability — 6-7-year-olds were mostly best fit by a random-response model on an integration structure, and a floored child produces a flat block and no rate at all. Reading demand is near-zero (badges are pictorial glyphs and the patterns are drawn), so unlike the invented-morphology designs this type has no decoding floor at K-1. Tap-one-of-five with large fixed targets keeps motor load off the rate.

adaptive.content_range: one transformation applied to two blocks (K-1) up to a chain of three, two of them re-orientations that do not commute, applied to seven blocks (6-8 and above level)
difficulty_levers: composition depth: how many badges the machine applies, 1 to 3 (dominant). Capped at 3 deliberately: a depth-4 chain has 360 badge relabellings rather than 120, and relabellings that collapse onto the key are what made FLU-OPCHAIN-01’s key derivable from content on 11 of 234 items

figure density: how many blocks the pattern holds, 2 to 7 — the range-extending lever, carrying roughly 6.4 of the 19 points of the scale. This is what lets composition depth stop at 3 while the bank still reaches 20, and it adds load without adding relabelling collapse, because tracking seven blocks through a rearrangement is harder than tracking two for a reason unrelated to how deep the composition is

number of orientation transformations in the chain, 0 to 2, each of which forces an imagined re-orientation rather than a local rearrangement. Value 0 is reachable at every depth, so no rung of the ladder requires a rotation
whether BOTH orientation transformations are in play, which is when reordering the chain changes the answer
representational mixing: whether the chain interleaves re-orientations with rearrangements, so an imagined pattern must be carried through steps that do not reorient it

distractor distance: how near the four wrong options sit to the key on a named partial-rule axis, from "applied two badges in the wrong order" down to "applied none" (the continuous within-rung positioner)
adaptive.levers_from_the_design_document_that_are: STAGE2_QUESTION_DESIGN §3.4 lists six levers and three of them are not properties of an item, so §1.1(d) forbids pricing them here. "Number of candidate transformations in play" is fixed for the whole block by §3.4 itself. "Whether the chain was previously demonstrated" is a property of a SEQUENCE, not of an item. "Whether the queried face or feature is visible in the input" presumes a three-dimensional block figure and an occlusion model; this design uses a two-dimensional lattice, where every block is always visible, so the lever has no referent. Figure density — §3.4’s own "figure complexity (block count)" — is promoted from a minor positioner to the principal range-extender in their place.

system_persistence.consistent: One badge-to-transformation mapping for the whole bank, so what the child learns on trial 1 is still true on trial 30 and knowledge of the system transfers across items. This is the measurement arm.
system_persistence.perTrial: A fresh mapping every item, so nothing carries forward. This is the SCRAMBLED CONTROL: any climb observed here is the design’s contamination floor — practice, warm-up, residual interface learning, guessing, regression at the handover and difficulty misspecification, summed. STAGE2_QUESTION_DESIGN §3.4 names this type the MOST LIKELY of the four to fail this control, because within-session rotation practice is a plausible source of a climb owing nothing to the hidden system, which is why the design holds the mapping-blind ceiling near chance rather than merely closing the brute-force leak.
system_persistence.why_a_mode_and_not_a_second_type: One generator emits both banks and one renderer serves both arms. Two generators or two renderers would confound the contrast with the generator or the renderer and the control would be measuring the wrong difference.
system_persistence.equated_across_arms: The transformation chain and the block patterns are drawn from the lever tuple and the seed, never from the mode, so the input pattern, all five option patterns, the key, the key slot, the distractor slate, the age band and the stated difficulty are identical item-for-item across the two banks. Only which badge symbols label the chain differs, and the badge tray is listed in one canonical order in both arms so the tray itself carries no information. Whatever rotation practice a child accrues therefore accrues equally in both arms and is differenced out by the gate.
system_persistence.where_the_banks_live: The consistent arm is research/exam-question-types/banks/SPA-XFORM-01.jsonl, inside the served directory. The scrambled arm is research/exam-question-types/control-banks/SPA-XFORM-01.perTrial.jsonl, outside it, because nothing is learnable in the control arm by construction and serving it to a child would administer a block with nothing to learn.

adaptive.notes: Difficulty is computed from the levers above by a signed, monotone formula and re-derived independently by check-SPA-XFORM-01.mjs, which also asserts monotonicity in every lever. That matters more here than for a standing type: the block serves different item subsets early and late, so difficulty error that correlates with subset composition correlates with trial index, and correlated error in difficulty maps straight onto the fitted rate — random labelling error only attenuates, structured labelling error biases. The bank carries 0.5-point grain across the whole 1-20 scale rather than the usual 1-point bins, because a fast climber ends the block asking for items several points above where it started and a pool that thins out saturates the fit. STATUS: SPECCED AND GENERATED, UNGATED. Gate A has not been run on this bank and the scrambled control is a binding acceptance criterion whose Gate B needs roughly 128 real children, so nothing about this type has been validated and it is not wired into the live learning block. Both banks ship syntheticOnly:true and validated:false.

engagement_hook: The machine will not tell you what its badges mean, so every trial is a guess you get to check — and the moment a badge clicks into place you can suddenly read chains that were gibberish a minute ago.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The dominant risk is SPATIAL PRACTICE masquerading as learning of the system, and STAGE2_QUESTION_DESIGN §3.4 names this type the most likely of the four to fail the scrambled control for exactly that reason: mental-rotation performance improves within a session for almost everyone, and a rate produced that way is indistinguishable inside the fit from a rate produced by induction. Four mitigations, all measured rather than asserted. (1) Rotation is one transformation of six and re-orientation two of six; the other four are rearrangements of the lattice that no amount of rotation skill performs, and the orientation count is a free lever whose value 0 is reachable at every depth, so 36% of the bank needs no re-orientation at all and no rung of the ladder requires one. (2) At least four of the five options on every item are patterns SOME injective badge relabelling produces, so a solver with perfect spatial execution and no knowledge of the mapping cannot narrow below 1-in-4 against a 1-in-5 chance baseline; the achieved mean is 0.246. (3) Neither ink nor displacement carries signal: every transformation is a permutation of the lattice cells so all five options show the same number of blocks, and at least one distractor moves exactly as many blocks as the key does, so "count the blocks" and "tap whichever picture moved the most" are both dead by construction. (4) Both arms serve identical patterns, so whatever practice accrues is differenced out. Scoring is accuracy only; response time is a diagnostic and never enters the fit. The second risk is INTERFACE LEARNING: the response grammar is borrowed from three S1 spatial types the child already completed, so the interface is paid for during bracketing; one tap with fixed option positions, so neither motor sequence nor position search is learnable; an unscored interface gate to k consecutive correct on depth-0 instances before trial 0; and the scrambled-control arm quantifies whatever residue survives all three. INDUCING OVER THE FURNITURE: a blind audit of FLU-OPCHAIN-01 found its `ring` transformation drawn as a rounded rectangle indistinguishable from a UI border, so children could have been learning the chrome rather than the figure. Closed structurally here — every transformation is a permutation of the 16 lattice cells and therefore cannot add, remove, enclose, outline or decorate anything; the only thing that ever changes is where the blocks are. The lexical half of the same audit forbids any transformation or badge named after interface furniture, and the renderer contract puts the lattice on faint dots rather than a ruled table. Pseudo-guessing: five options with correct-key positions allocated round-robin, so the modal-key advantage sits at +0.1pt over the 20% arithmetic floor for a five-option item, and every distractor is a plausible system-failure rather than filler. CONTENT-COMPUTABLE SHORTCUTS are closed explicitly and counted: a client that brute-forces every badge relabelling recovers the key on 0 of 234 items, against the 11 of 234 the reference type shipped with. Attributes are positional only — there is no colour, fill or size anywhere in the vocabulary — so colour-vision differences do not gate the task, and no transformation is invisible on a symmetric pattern because any chain that leaves the pattern where it was is rejected. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); this type’s stimuli are figural, so its reading demand is limited to the instruction line, which uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback). Stated construct-purity cost, not hidden: §3.4 expects chains to load on working-memory span as well as spatial ability, because the intermediate pattern must be held in mind, and figure density loads the same way. That is a cost of the design, and §3.4’s own failure test (c) — chain-length accuracy tracking a WM span measure more tightly than trial index — remains the check for it.

name: Home Again (object-location binding)
topics_techniques_covered: visuospatial_span_picture_recognition
visuospatial_span_corsi_forward
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Watch which animal lives in which house, then after they come out and shuffle put each animal back in its own house.
interaction: During encoding, N distinct animals each appear briefly in a distinct house on a 3x3 grid, then vanish. The animals reappear in a tray; the child taps an animal then taps its remembered house (tap a filled house to send its animal back). When all are placed the bindings are scored and the set size adapts up on a fully-correct round.
self_teach: Wordless demo: two animals show in their houses, vanish, and a ghost hand taps each animal then its house (turning green); one unscored 2-animal warm-up before scoring. Pure tap-tap, no reading.

learning_science.principle: Feature/relational binding in working memory (episodic buffer)
learning_science.why: Item-to-location binding taxes the episodic buffer and relational memory, dissociable from serial-order or item-only span and closely tied to fluid reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score WHICH animal goes WHERE (binding), not the order of visits; the error taxonomy separates swaps (mis-binding) from empty-house (lost-location) errors.
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. (2000). The episodic buffer: a new component of working memory? Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

learning_science.principle: Associative/relational memory
learning_science.why: Binding distinct identities to distinct locations is a relational-memory operation that adds tail variance beyond storage capacity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use distinct objects (not one repeated token) so each placement is an identity-location association.
learning_science.source: Cohen, N. & Eichenbaum, H. (1993). Memory, Amnesia, and the Hippocampal System.

learning_science.principle: Adaptive span staircase; accuracy over speed
learning_science.why: Consistency of correct binding, not speed, is the ability signal (worst-performance logic).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Set size staircases 1-up/1-down above grade; first-placement latency is logged as planning and never rewarded as speed; consistency across matched set sizes is reported.
learning_science.source: Conway, A. et al. (2005). Working memory span tasks: a methodological review. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review.

tail_precision_rationale: Binding span (M-SPAN/M-DIFFREACH via an above-grade set-size staircase) keeps separating high performers who all ceiling on short lists, and the swap-vs-empty error split (M-ERRTYPE) reveals whether failures are mis-bindings (identities kept, associations scrambled) or lost locations - a finer grain than a right/wrong span. Consistency across matched set sizes (M-CONSIST) lowers the conditional error at the cut.
age_rationale: Tap-to-place with large targets and set size 2 suits K-1; the above-grade staircase (up to ~6-8 bindings) gives headroom for 6-8. No timed pressure and no fine motor beyond tapping.

adaptive.content_range: 2 up to ~8 item-location bindings on a 3x3 (extensible) grid
adaptive.difficulty_levers: set size; encoding time; grid size / spatial proximity of houses; visual similarity of animals; optional retention delay
adaptive.notes: Fully procedural: sample distinct objects and distinct cells; matched parallel forms clone trivially for consistency estimates.

engagement_hook: The animals come out to play and mix themselves up - a warm 'everyone home!' puzzle where getting them all back feels great.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (tap-tap only, large targets); verbal labeling could aid rehearsal (use hard-to-name similar animals at high bands); spatial-only strategies (distinct identities force binding, not pure location memory); scale encoding time with set size so it measures binding, not exposure. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Firefly Trail (spatial span)
topics_techniques_covered: visuospatial_span_corsi_forward
visuospatial_span_corsi_backward
visuospatial_span_picture_recognition
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Fireflies (tiles) light up one-by-one in a growing sequence and the child taps them back in the same order, or in reverse.
interaction: N tiles in a 3x3 grid flash sequentially; the child reproduces the sequence by tapping tiles, and a Backward toggle asks for reverse order. Re-tapping a selected tile de-selects it (logged as a revision). The trial auto-submits at N taps; span rises by 1 after a correct trial and drops by 1 after an error (Levitt 1-up/1-down staircase).
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand watches three tiles flash then taps them in order and shows a check mark (about 6s), followed by one unscored warm-up trial; no text is required.

learning_science.principle: Corsi block-tapping visuospatial span
learning_science.why: A standardized, language-free index of visuospatial short-term memory that dissociates from verbal span.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a 3x3 tile grid with sequential lighting and same-order tap-back as the core mechanic.
learning_science.source: Kessels, R. P. C., van Zandvoort, M. J. E., Postma, A., Kappelle, L. J., & de Haan, E. H. F. (2000). The Corsi Block-Tapping Task: standardization and normative data. Applied Neuropsychology, 7(4), 252-258.

learning_science.principle: Capacity limit of about four chunks
learning_science.why: Working-memory capacity centers near 3-5 items, so a staircase around this range maximizes information at the tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Start span at 3 and adapt by plus/minus 1; extend the item bank to spans 8-9 for above-level probing.
learning_science.source: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.

learning_science.principle: Forward vs backward span dissociation
learning_science.why: Backward reproduction adds central-executive manipulation beyond passive storage.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer a Backward mode and report the forward-minus-backward manipulation cost.
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), The Psychology of Learning and Motivation (Vol. 8, pp. 47-89). Academic Press.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Memory span threshold
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The staircase-estimated longest sequence a child reliably reproduces is a continuous, fine-grained capacity index that keeps separating high performers who all hit ceiling on fixed-length items.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Track the highest sequence length reproduced correctly under a 1-up/1-down span staircase; average the last several reversal lengths.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: 6-10 adaptive trials per mode (forward/backward) for a stable threshold.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Manipulation cost
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The drop from forward (storage) span to backward/reorder (manipulation) span isolates central-executive manipulation, which tracks fluid reasoning better than raw storage at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Compute forward max span minus backward or sorted max span under matched staircases.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Enough trials in each mode to estimate both spans (6-10 each).

tail_precision_rationale: Reproduction accuracy is dichotomous and saturates fast among gifted children, so this type extracts tail signal from process: the staircase-estimated span threshold (M-SPAN) and max reached (M-DIFFREACH) give a continuous capacity index above grade level, forward-minus-backward manipulation cost (M-MANIPCOST) isolates executive manipulation from passive storage, and consistency measures (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) plus order-vs-item error typing (M-ERRTYPE) separate secure high-capacity solvers from lucky ones by scoring on lapses rather than raw speed.
age_rationale: Wordless, tap-only and language-free, so it runs from K-1 (framed as catching fireflies, spans 2-3) upward; older bands unlock the Backward mode and spans of 6-9. Targets are large (66px) to remove fine-motor demands for little hands; only tapping (no drag) is required.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 short forward spans (2-3) with animal framing up to 6-8 backward spans of 8-9 and denser grids
adaptive.difficulty_levers: sequence length, forward vs backward, presentation rate, grid size, optional delayed spatial-recognition array variant
adaptive.notes: Span is a native psychophysical staircase and sequences are procedurally generated, so unlimited matched clones exist for M-CONSIST parallel forms.

engagement_hook: A glowing firefly trail that visibly grows each time you succeed, so leveling up feels like lighting a longer and longer path.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: tap accuracy on small or close tiles (mitigated by large targets, tap-not-drag). Familiarity: Simon-style novelty (mitigated by ghost-hand plus warm-up). Attention/ADHD: sustained attention and impulsivity can depress span and inflate variability, mimicking low capacity; flag by gating on M-ENGAGE/M-DRIFT and treating occasional lapses as process signal rather than capacity, requiring consistency across trials before a tail decision. Device: touch vs mouse latency and screen size affect tile spacing. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Gatekeeper (probed running span / continuous updating)
topics_techniques_covered: running_memory_span
memory_updating_numeric
memory_updating_keep_track
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Creatures parade through a gate one at a time and, at unpredictable checkpoints, a guard asks the child to tap back the last few that just passed - then the parade resumes and is probed again.
interaction: A single continuous stream of creatures crosses the gate at a fixed rate. At random moments the gate closes and a checkpoint panel appears; the child taps the last k creatures in order from a palette, the panel clears, and the SAME stream resumes toward the next checkpoint. A stream contains several probes, so the child must keep a rolling window live throughout (not a single terminal recall). A numeric shell streams digits with occasional operations and probes the current running value; a keep-track shell probes the most recent creature of each colour/family. k adapts up after a clean checkpoint and down after an error.
self_teach: A ghost-hand watches three creatures pass, the gate closes, and the hand taps the last two in order with a check (about 7s); one unscored warm-up probe follows. The repeated close-and-ask makes 'always hold the most recent ones' self-teaching.

learning_science.principle: Running memory span with unpredictable probes
learning_science.why: Not knowing when (or how often) recall will be required forces continuous updating of only the most recent items, isolating updating from list memorisation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probe the last k at multiple random points within one ongoing stream rather than once at the end.
learning_science.source: Pollack, I., Johnson, L. B., & Knaff, P. R. (1959). Running memory span. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 57(3), 137-146.

learning_science.principle: Memory updating as a distinct executive function
learning_science.why: Repeatedly discarding superseded contents and inserting new ones is a separable updating component of executive function.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use repeated mid-stream probes and a numeric-update shell so contents must be continually overwritten.
learning_science.source: Miyake, A., Friedman, N. P., Emerson, M. J., Witzki, A. H., Howerter, A., & Wager, T. D. (2000). The unity and diversity of executive functions and their contributions to complex frontal lobe tasks. Cognitive Psychology, 41(1), 49-100.

learning_science.principle: Recency and the rolling focus of attention
learning_science.why: Accuracy across serial positions within the rolling window reveals how many recent items sit in the immediately accessible focus.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score a recency gradient across probes and vary k to map the accessible window.
learning_science.source: Oberauer, K. (2002). Access to information in working memory: exploring the focus of attention. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 28(3), 411-421.

tail_precision_rationale: Repeated within-stream probing yields signal a single terminal recall cannot: the accuracy-by-k slope across many probes (M-UPDATECOST) is a direct updating-efficiency index, partial-credit position scoring (M-POLY) builds a recency gradient that localises the accessible window, intrusion-vs-novel error typing (M-ERRTYPE) exposes proactive-interference control, and response-time variability and lapses across probes (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) capture worst-performance consistency; drift and engagement (M-DRIFT, M-ENGAGE) gate the many-probe stream so tail decisions rest on engaged, consistent updating rather than speed.
age_rationale: Holding and re-reporting the last 2 across surprise probes is feasible at 2-3; multi-family keep-track and numeric running-value updating demand more control and are reserved for 4-5 and 6-8. Continuous updating with withholding across many probes overloads most K-1 children, so the floor is 2-3 with the last-2 creature shell. Interaction is tap-only from a fixed palette; the numeric shell assumes simple addition and is age-gated.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 last-2 creatures with sparse probes up to 6-8 last-4 with dense probes, numeric running-value updates and multi-family keep-track
adaptive.difficulty_levers: k, probe frequency and unpredictability, stream rate, numeric-update step size, number of families, palette similarity
adaptive.notes: Streams, probe schedules and numeric operations are generated and k is a native staircase; many probes per stream yield stable within-stream slopes and matched parallel forms.

engagement_hook: A guard-the-gate game of surprise checkpoints: you never know when the gate will slam shut and quiz you, so staying ready and nailing each spot-check feels like beating a memory ambush.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attention/ADHD: surprise probes load sustained attention and impulse control, so scores must be read with consistency and M-ENGAGE/M-DRIFT gating, not as raw capacity. Numeracy: the numeric shell needs addition (age-gated). Motor: single taps from a fixed palette, no drag. Familiarity: the close-and-ask rhythm is novel but self-teaches via the ghost-hand and warm-up. Startle: the gate-close should be gentle (no loud or sudden effects) to avoid penalising sensitive children. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Star Grid (simultaneous visuospatial span / change detection)
topics_techniques_covered: visuospatial_span_picture_recognition
visuospatial_span_corsi_forward
spatial_visualization: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: A pattern of coloured stars flashes on a grid all at once, disappears, and after a short delay the child says whether a probed cell is the SAME or CHANGED - or taps back which cells were lit.
interaction: A set of coloured stars appears simultaneously across grid cells for a brief exposure (about 700ms) then blanks. After a short retention delay the test display returns and one cell is probed: the child taps SAME if its colour is unchanged or CHANGED if it differs (change-detection shell). A recognition shell instead asks the child to tap all the cells that had been lit (order optional). Set size (number of stars) rises after correct responses and falls after errors (staircase), and hits and false alarms feed a visual-capacity estimate. RT and accuracy are logged, but scoring is capacity/consistency-based, not speeded.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand watches a three-star flash, waits through the blank, sees the probe turn a different colour, and taps CHANGED with a check (about 7s); one unscored warm-up follows. The flash-then-probe rhythm teaches 'remember the picture, spot the change' with no text.

learning_science.principle: Capacity of visual working memory
learning_science.why: Simultaneous arrays with change detection estimate the number of integrated objects held in visual WM, a capacity limited to a few items.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use brief simultaneous arrays and single-probe change detection to estimate visual capacity K.
learning_science.source: Luck, S. J., & Vogel, E. K. (1997). The capacity of visual working memory for features and conjunctions. Nature, 390(6657), 279-281.

learning_science.principle: Signal-detection estimate of capacity
learning_science.why: Modelling hits and false alarms yields a bias-free sensitivity/capacity index rather than confounding cautious and guessing responders.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Compute sensitivity (d-prime) and a capacity K from hit and false-alarm rates across set sizes.
learning_science.source: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: a reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.

learning_science.principle: Development of visual working-memory capacity
learning_science.why: Change-detection capacity increases across childhood and is a sensitive, language-free individual-difference measure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Staircase set size and report capacity to track above-grade capacity in older children.
learning_science.source: Simmering, V. R. (2012). The development of visual working memory capacity during early childhood. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 111(4), 695-707.

tail_precision_rationale: Simultaneous change detection extracts a continuous capacity signal that sequential span and dichotomous accuracy miss: signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) yields a bias-free visual-capacity K that separates cautious from guessing responders, the staircase set-size threshold (M-SPAN) and highest set size reached (M-DIFFREACH) give an above-grade capacity index, and change-vs-no-change error typing (M-ERRTYPE) with cross-form consistency (M-CONSIST) and lapse rate (M-LAPSE) score stable capacity rather than speed - RT is logged only as process, never credited.
age_rationale: Simultaneous change detection is a two-choice same/changed judgment that works from K-1 with small set sizes (2-3 stars) and scales to large set sizes (6-8 items) with shorter exposures and longer delays for older children. Presentation is simultaneous (no sequence to reproduce), so it complements the sequential Corsi span; targets are large well-spaced grid cells requiring only a tap.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 set size 2-3 with generous exposure up to 6-8 set sizes of 6+ with brief exposure, longer delay and a recognition-reproduction shell
adaptive.difficulty_levers: set size, exposure duration, retention delay, colour/shape similarity of items, change magnitude, single-probe vs whole-array recognition
adaptive.notes: Arrays, probes and change trials are generated with controlled change rates and set size is a native staircase; enough change and no-change trials per set size are needed for a stable d-prime and capacity K.

engagement_hook: A spot-the-difference star flash: the sky lights up for a blink and you catch whether a star changed, so holding the whole picture in your mind's eye feels like a superpower.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Colour vision: change detection uses highly distinct hues and offers a shape-change and position-recognition alternate so colour-blind children are not disadvantaged. Attention/ADHD: brief exposures load attention; gate on M-ENGAGE and require consistency before tail calls. Vision/device: exposure duration depends on display refresh, so the demo logs frame time and uses conservative exposures. Motor: single taps on large cells. Familiarity mitigated by the ghost-hand and warm-up. Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: Question Quest
topics_techniques_covered: curiosity
divergent_thinking
observed question-asking and exploration
ask-and-guess task
receptive_vocabulary: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: Shown a strange, intriguing picture, the child asks as many questions about it as they can and guesses what caused it and what might happen next.
interaction: An odd scene appears (a door in a tree, a puddle that glows). The child builds questions by tapping starter cards (Who / What / Where / Why / How / What if) and finishing them, or types them freely; separate rounds invite 'guess why this happened' and 'guess what happens next.' The engine logs the number of questions, their depth (surface what/who vs causal why/how vs hypothetical what-if), and the fluency and variety of the cause and consequence guesses. Every question and guess is welcomed; none is wrong.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows the scene, then a hand tapping the 'Why...?' card and a question bubble popping up, then a 'What if...?' card with another bubble - cueing 'ask lots of questions about it.' One unscored warm-up scene lets the child ask two questions before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Ask-and-guess (asking questions and guessing causes and consequences about a picture) is a validated divergent-thinking task
learning_science.why: It elicits question generation and hypothesis generation - forms of ideational fluency that alternate-uses and consequences prompts do not directly sample
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score fluency and variety of the child's questions and guesses about an intriguing stimulus rather than a single keyed answer
learning_science.source: Torrance, E. P. (1974). Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking: Norms-Technical Manual. Bensenville, IL: Scholastic Testing Service.

learning_science.principle: Spontaneous question-asking is a direct behavioral index of epistemic curiosity and drives learning
learning_science.why: The rate and depth of a child's questions during a novel activity reflect an intrinsic drive to close information gaps that reasoning tests cannot see
learning_science.concrete_decision: Count questions and rate their depth (surface fact vs causal vs hypothetical) as the curiosity signal (M-QUERY) instead of a curiosity questionnaire
learning_science.source: Engel, S. (2011). Children's need to know: Curiosity in schools. Harvard Educational Review, 81(4), 625-645.

learning_science.principle: Children's questions are a mechanism for gathering information and building knowledge
learning_science.why: Information-seeking questions, especially causal ones, mark active knowledge construction and predict who pursues understanding on their own
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distinguish information-seeking causal/explanatory questions from mere labeling questions when scoring depth
learning_science.source: Chouinard, M. M. (2007). Children's questions: A mechanism for cognitive development. Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development, 72(1), 1-129.

tail_precision_rationale: CogAT observes what a child does when told exactly what to do; it never observes the questions a child asks when facing the unknown. M-QUERY (count and depth of questions) is a direct epistemic-curiosity axis, and grading question depth - causal/hypothetical over labeling - separates children who probe mechanism from those who merely name. The guess rounds add M-IDEAFLU, M-FLEX (variety of causal and consequential explanations), and M-ORIG (rare-but-plausible guesses) so the same activity yields both a curiosity and a divergent-thinking signal. At the gifted tail this distinguishes an able-but-incurious child from an able-and-inquisitive one, and it does so through question generation rather than the physical exploration and uncertainty-choice mechanic of the Mystery Box. M-ENGAGE confirms questioning reflects interest, not idle tapping.
age_rationale: Composing questions on screen depends on emerging question syntax and enough language to fill starter cards, more reliable from about grade 2; K-1 curiosity is captured behaviorally by the tactile Mystery Box instead. From grade 2 up, starter-card scaffolds support 2-3 while 4-5 and 6-8 compose freely, and prompts are voiced for early readers. (D-017: audio is not used — deliver as simple on-screen text; reading is required.)

adaptive.content_range: simple single-oddity scenes (young) up to rich scenes with many possible questions and subtler anomalies (older)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: scene complexity and ambiguity, number of embedded anomalies, whether cause and consequence guessing is required, question-window length
adaptive.notes: Difficulty is depth of possible inquiry, not correctness: branch to richer, more ambiguous scenes for children who ask many deep questions so the ceiling of inquiry is probed rather than a theta on accuracy.

engagement_hook: A mysterious scene that begs 'what is going on here?', where every question the child asks lights up the picture and reveals a tiny hint - curiosity is immediately rewarded with a peek behind the mystery.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Question quantity confounds with verbal ability and question syntax (use starter-card scaffolds and voicing; score depth, not word count); shy or reticent children may under-ask even when curious (corroborate with the Mystery Box behavioral signals); scene-content familiarity shapes what feels puzzling (rotate novel scenes); depth rating of questions can be subjective (use a clear causal-vs-labeling rubric and audit). Reading policy (D-017): reading is a REQUIRED baseline-literacy capability, not a construct-irrelevant risk to mitigate — instructions and stimuli are on-screen text only (never audio); K-1 uses very simple, high-frequency words a beginning reader can interpret; a child who cannot read the grade-appropriate text is intentionally screened out (capability-to-benefit from reading-based Timeback).

name: What Would You Do?
topics_techniques_covered: situational_judgment
social-emotional situational judgment
task-approach/conscientiousness situational judgment
complementary:social_emotional_competence
inference_reading_comprehension: full content-range coverage across this type's difficulty spectrum (recat full-range retag)
one_liner: A short animated scene shows a tricky social or school situation, and the child taps the character action they think works best (then sees what happens next).
interaction: An illustrated/animated scenario plays (voiced for pre-readers), pausing to offer 2-4 pictured action choices. The child taps a choice; the scene branches to show a consequence, sometimes leading to a follow-up decision. Responses are keyed against an expert-consensus effectiveness scale (partial credit for good-but-not-best options). The engine logs choice, decision time, how long options are inspected before choosing, and any changes of mind.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand demo (<=10s) shows a scene of a dropped lunch tray, a hand tapping the 'help pick it up' character over the 'walk away' character, and a happy outcome - cueing 'tap the best thing the character could do.' One unscored warm-up scenario is played and discussed with a neutral outcome before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Situational judgment tests validly assess practical/social judgment via response to realistic scenarios
learning_science.why: Judgment and social-emotional competence predict adjustment and achievement but are untouched by abstract reasoning items
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use branching scenario items keyed to an expert-consensus effectiveness scale (partial credit) rather than a single right answer
learning_science.source: McDaniel, M. A., Morgeson, F. P., Finnegan, E. B., Campion, M. A., & Braverman, E. P. (2001). Use of situational judgment tests to predict job performance. Journal of Applied Psychology, 86(4), 730-740.

learning_science.principle: Task-approach judgment (how one handles hard, boring, or frustrating work) reflects conscientiousness and self-regulation
learning_science.why: A child who chooses persistence/help-seeking strategies in scenarios reveals dispositions that predict school success
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include conscientiousness scenarios ('your project is hard and boring - what do you do?') scored for effective self-regulatory choices
learning_science.source: Duckworth, A. L., & Seligman, M. E. P. (2005). Self-discipline outdoes IQ in predicting academic performance of adolescents. Psychological Science, 16(12), 939-944.

learning_science.principle: Animated, low-reading situational judgment can assess young children's social decision-making in a game
learning_science.why: Interactive branching scenarios reduce the reading load and increase ecological validity for social-emotional skills
learning_science.concrete_decision: Deliver scenarios as voiced animations with pictured choices and branching consequences (stealth SEL) for K-1
learning_science.source: DeRosier, M. E., & Thomas, J. M. (2019). Establishing the criterion validity of Zoo U's game-based social-emotional skills assessment. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment, 37(3), 341-354.

tail_precision_rationale: Reasoning cutoffs ignore social/practical judgment entirely. Keying scenarios to an expert-consensus scale yields a graded score (M-POLY) rather than dichotomous right/wrong, extracting tail information from each rich item.
